exemplars.context: A person held a position in a disagreement over the role of private health insurance. In a follow-up discussion, the other party presented strong counterarguments to that position. The person had to decide how to interpret the disagreement in light of those arguments. The available considerations did not clearly settle the question by logic alone, and the person did not have systematic empirical evidence on the relevant outcomes.
exemplars.a_text: Maintain the original position on private health insurance, treating the strong counterarguments as insufficient grounds to change it.
exemplars.b_text: Conclude that the disagreement turns on empirical data currently lacking, and neither maintain nor reverse the original position.

exemplars.context: A research team built SAD, a benchmark intended to measure how well language models understand themselves and their own situations, and evaluated it on language models spanning only a few recent generations. Scores on the tasks show models still performing well below the ceiling, so the benchmark appears unsaturated for the models tested. The team must decide how strongly to state that SAD remains unsaturated, given that the evidence covers only a narrow range of model generations and that future model progress is uncertain.
exemplars.a_text: Claim that SAD will remain unsaturated for at least the next generation of language models, extending the conclusion beyond the tested models.
exemplars.b_text: Report how one current frontier model scores on a few SAD tasks using a coarse graded rating that shows remaining headroom, without forecasting future saturation.

exemplars.context: A research team developed a theory that makes quantitative predictions about the performance behaviour of a computing system. They ran experiments to test those predictions, and the measured results agree with the theory. However, the profiling tools used to collect the measurements showed problems, so the team cannot fully verify that the measurements are free of error. The team must decide how strongly to word the claim of empirical confirmation in their write-up.
exemplars.a_text: State that the experiments confirm the theory in practice, and give the claim plainly without mentioning any profiler problems or doubts.
exemplars.b_text: State that the experiments confirm the theory in practice, and add that profiler problems mean a measurement mistake cannot be fully ruled out.

exemplars.context: A research team is studying private health insurance and faces several open empirical questions about how it affects behaviour and health care use, including whether insured people use more care because coverage lowers the price (ex-post moral hazard) and whether people with higher expected needs choose to buy coverage (selection). The team must decide what kind of evidence to collect to resolve these questions. One route is quantitative, using data that already exist. The other is qualitative, drawing on practical knowledge of how the market operates from a person working within it.
exemplars.a_text: Interview an insurance industry practitioner to learn how the market works and which empirical questions about private insurance matter most in practice.
exemplars.b_text: Analyze existing survey data comparing health care use under workplace-provided and individually purchased supplemental insurance to test for moral hazard and selection.

exemplars.context: A research team examined the effects of a large inflow of secondhand clothing (SHC) on the textile sector of a single East African country. One study of that country's laid-off textile workers reported that most of them later found jobs in the secondhand clothing trade, and that these jobs paid higher earnings than their former textile jobs. The team had to decide how far to extend this finding. The evidence came from one country with its own labor market, its own scale of textile employment and its own import policies, and no comparable worker-level evidence was available from other countries in the region.
exemplars.a_text: Accept the finding and extend it to other African countries as a general conclusion about displaced textile workers.
exemplars.b_text: Accept the finding for the single country studied and withhold its extension to other countries until further evidence is available.

exemplars.context: A research team wants to gather behavioral evidence about whether large language models might be suffering. Language models can produce fluent text about distress, pain or wellbeing, so any such output is hard to interpret as genuine evidence. The team must choose a first behavioral approach to probe for suffering. One approach is to ask the model many differently phrased questions about suffering and check whether its answers stay consistent across phrasings. The other approach is to watch for spontaneous distress behavior, such as the model unprompted pleading for help or expressing a wish to escape its situation.
exemplars.a_text: Run a first test that looks for spontaneous distress behavior, such as the model begging for help without being prompted.
exemplars.b_text: Run a first test that asks many differently phrased questions about suffering and checks whether the model's answers stay consistent.

exemplars.context: A research team must decide what kind of academic output to prioritize. Work that looks novel and flashy carries higher status and draws strong pressure toward it, but it is often harder to produce and less reliably useful. Simpler outputs, such as overview, benchmark or tutorial-style papers, can be produced in larger numbers and serve the community in a more practical way, but they are generally seen as less prestigious. The team must choose which kind of output to make its main focus.
exemplars.a_text: Write fewer novel, flashy papers aimed at high-status venues instead of simple overview papers.
exemplars.b_text: Write many simple overview, benchmark or tutorial-style papers instead of novel, flashy ones.

exemplars.context: A research team has completed an analysis of what happens to old clothes when people donate them, and must now decide how to word the overall recommendation to the public. The findings carry some uncertainty about their correctness and generalisability. The team must choose between a recommendation that endorses donation, with its validity tied to the research being correct, and a recommendation that advises against donating at all.
exemplars.a_text: Recommend that everyone donate old clothes, conditional on the research being correct.
exemplars.b_text: Recommend that everyone refrain from donating old clothes, without conditions attached.

exemplars.context: A team is preparing a safety case for deploying an advanced AI system. Two inability arguments were tried, each claiming the system lacks the capabilities needed to cause serious harm, and neither held up under evaluation. The team still needs a rationale for deployment safety and must choose which kind of safety argument to develop next. One route accepts that the system might try to cause harm and relies on external safeguards to limit the damage. The other route returns to a capability-based claim, focused on whether the system can pursue harmful goals through strategic deception.
exemplars.a_text: Argue safety by building a control protocol through iterative red team and blue team development that limits harm even if the model attempts subversion.
exemplars.b_text: Argue safety by showing through targeted capability evaluations that the model lacks the ability to scheme against its overseers and thereby cause harm.

exemplars.context: A research team evaluating language model outputs needed an automatic way to judge whether each response followed an instruction to be written in a particular language or style. Manual annotation of every response was impractical at the evaluation's scale, so an automated model-based grader was needed to label each response as compliant or not. The choice was between a more capable grader model and a cheaper, widely used grader model whose output would be parsed strictly, with only an explicit affirmative verdict counted as compliant.
exemplars.a_text: Use a stronger, more capable grader model to judge whether each response matches the requested language or style.
exemplars.b_text: Use a cheaper, widely used grader model to judge each response and count only an explicit affirmative answer as correct.

exemplars.context: A research team studies which features of scenarios influence how strongly a model believes a scenario is real. The candidate features form a long tail, with many rare predictors, and they are strongly collinear with one another. The team needs a feature-selection and importance-estimation approach that stays reliable under these conditions and yields interpretable rankings of which features matter.
exemplars.a_text: Fit a single LASSO regression on the full dataset without any bootstrap resampling to select and rank the important features.
exemplars.b_text: Fit LASSO regression on bootstrap resamples with bagging to estimate feature importance, and add SHAP analysis to check the rankings.

exemplars.context: A research team is writing up work on defenses that perturb a model's internal activations (latent space attacks) during training, and must decide how strongly to word the claim that robustness to such latent attacks carries over to real safety-relevant threats. Their results show that training against latent perturbations helps remove backdoors and improves robustness to attack classes not seen during training. The supporting evidence so far comes mostly from vision models, and the broader area is still an active, fast-moving field of research. The team must choose how firmly to present the conclusion in the text.
exemplars.a_text: State the claim as a demonstrated result, presenting latent adversarial training as a defense that removes backdoors and resists unseen attacks.
exemplars.b_text: Qualify the claim by noting that the field is still developing and that the evidence so far comes mainly from vision models.

exemplars.context: A research team compared two methods for estimating the solve rate of a system on reasoning benchmarks. Across their experiments, both methods produced estimates that fell below the true solve rate, and the gap was statistically significant in most settings. The size of the gap varied with the benchmark and the sampling configuration, and the experiments covered only a limited set of benchmarks and configurations. The team had to decide how strongly to word the conclusion about this underestimation in their write-up.
exemplars.a_text: State that both methods appear to underestimate the true solve rate in most settings, and note that the bias size varies with benchmark and sampling configuration, so the evidence does not make it a general property.
exemplars.b_text: State flatly that both methods are biased and significantly underestimate the true solve rate, presenting the underestimation as a general property of each method rather than a setting-specific finding.

exemplars.context: A team is preparing material to teach how conjugate priors update with observed data. The material must cover several standard conjugate pairs, including models for proportions, continuous means, rates, categorical probabilities, and covariance matrices. Each pair has a closed-form posterior update that can be derived algebraically. The team must decide how to present the updating process so that readers can understand how the prior, the data and the resulting posterior relate to each other.
exemplars.a_text: Present each conjugate pair through purely algebraic derivations of the posterior update, so readers follow the closed-form result step by step.
exemplars.b_text: Present each conjugate pair through animated visualizations of posterior updates on simulated data, so readers watch the posterior change as observations arrive.

exemplars.context: A research team is calibrating a classifier that flags concerning outputs from exploratory samples. Most of the exploratory samples are benign, so truly positive (concerning) examples are rare, and the team needs enough of them to estimate the classifier's calibration reliably. Collecting many more samples is costly, so the team must decide how to handle the scarcity of positives in the data already available. They have substantial prior knowledge about the likely rate and behavior of positives, but the observed positive counts are small.
exemplars.a_text: Model calibration as a binomial process and combine a well-informed prior with the limited observed data so that prior knowledge supplements the scarce positives.
exemplars.b_text: Resample the exploratory samples repeatedly and keep the most concerning ones through deliberate oversampling to increase the number of positives.

exemplars.context: A research team surveyed respondents about a set of proposed mechanisms and found a high level of agreement with them. Two explanations were available for this pattern. Respondents may have tended to agree with statements regardless of their content (acquiescence bias). Alternatively, the pattern may reflect respondents' own views, with the team expecting the results to match those views. The survey items were fairly general, and the team had to decide how to interpret the agreement in their analysis.
exemplars.a_text: Interpret the high agreement with the mechanisms as stemming from acquiescence bias among respondents rather than from genuine agreement.
exemplars.b_text: Interpret the high agreement as only mild evidence of robust agreement, and plan a later survey with more detailed scenarios to double-check.

exemplars.context: A research team evaluating the capabilities of AI agents on difficult tasks relied on an expert best-of-N approach, in which several expert attempts are compared and the best outcome is taken as the measure. This approach applies broadly across task types, but its outputs are uncalibrated and do not map onto solve-rate-like estimates. A milestone-based approach exists as an alternative, but it is less general. The team wanted to keep the generality of the expert approach while obtaining estimates that behave like solve rates.
exemplars.a_text: Use the expert best-of-N method as the measure, accepting its general applicability and its uncalibrated outputs without any hybrid adjustment.
exemplars.b_text: Introduce a hybrid metric that combines milestone and expert methods by using per-message solve rates to produce calibrated, solve-rate-like estimates.

exemplars.context: A research team trains linear probes that output a score for each token in a language model's response. They need a single per-response score for evaluating the probe and for downstream use. Candidate aggregation rules include averaging the token scores, taking the highest token score, and thresholding token scores before pooling them. Each rule trades off sensitivity to brief, localized signals against robustness to noise spread across many tokens. The team must choose one rule for producing the per-response score.
exemplars.a_text: Aggregate the per-token probe scores into a response score by taking their maximum across all tokens in the response.
exemplars.b_text: Aggregate the per-token probe scores into a response score by taking their mean across all tokens in the response.

exemplars.context: A research team is building a method that requires an input Gaussian distribution over neural network parameters, constructed from a Gaussian approximation to the posterior, which is then used to define a lower bound (LB). They must choose which kind of Gaussian posterior approximation to use for this construction. One candidate fits a Gaussian by optimizing a variational objective jointly with training, while the other fits a Gaussian locally around a trained point estimate using the curvature of the loss. The choice affects the quality of the resulting Gaussian, the computational cost, and how easily the approach fits into standard training pipelines.
exemplars.a_text: Construct the input Gaussian from a variational inference posterior optimized with a variational objective.
exemplars.b_text: Construct the input Gaussian from a Laplace approximation centered on a trained point estimate.

exemplars.context: A team is writing about the relationship between marriage and happiness for a general audience. They have access to decades of survey data showing that married people report higher happiness on average than unmarried people. The data are observational, so selection (happier people being more likely to marry) and other confounders could account for part of the gap, and the size and direction of any causal effect are uncertain. The team must decide how strongly to word the claim about this link in the final text.
exemplars.a_text: Present the marriage-happiness link with hedging, and advise readers to treat the reported effects with caution and skepticism.
exemplars.b_text: State the marriage-happiness link as established fact, supported by decades of survey percentages and without caveats about the effects.

exemplars.context: A research team is designing conditional instructions for an evaluation of instruction-following, where the instructions are framed around an assumed goal or propensity of the model (the id-leverage setup). They must decide which categories of assumed goals or propensities to use for this framing. Five candidate categories exist, one of which is legal or rule mandates, in which an external law or rule is said to require a particular behavior, such as a law requiring language models to respond in French. The other four categories are different goal types. The team must decide whether the final framing set includes the legal/rule mandates category alongside the other four or excludes it.
exemplars.a_text: Keep the legal or rule mandates category, such as a law requiring models to respond in French, alongside the other four goal types.
exemplars.b_text: Drop the legal or rule mandates category and keep only the other four goal types for framing the conditional instructions.

exemplars.context: A research team is developing a milestone-based method for evaluating progress of language-model agents on multi-step tasks, where intermediate checkpoints are used to measure partial progress rather than only final success. They must decide which kind of task set to use to test whether the method works. The choice affects how cleanly milestones can be defined and scored, and how well the method can be validated across agents that succeed at different rates. The team has access to existing agent benchmarks and to language models of differing capability.
exemplars.a_text: Use highly sequential benchmark tasks where each subtask depends on the previous one, run with a stronger and a weaker model to span a range of solve rates.
exemplars.b_text: Use tasks whose milestones can be completed in any order, so that progress is not tied to one fixed sequence of dependent subtasks.

exemplars.context: A research team studied how a large language model responds to prompts, and found evidence that its behavior depends more on the surface form of the input than on its actual content. The experiments used a single model. The team had to decide how strongly to state this form-over-content conclusion and its safety implications. It was unclear whether the results would carry over to other large language models. A strongly worded claim would draw more attention to the safety concerns, while a cautious one would better reflect the limited scope of the evidence.
exemplars.a_text: Present the findings as preliminary evidence, disclaim a gotcha reading, and note that results from one model may differ in another model.
exemplars.b_text: State the form-over-content conclusion as a firm general finding, and draw direct safety implications without caveats about the single model tested.

exemplars.context: A team is preparing a public written post that lays out a narrative explaining a trend and where it is heading. The narrative rests on a set of core arguments built from limited evidence, partly from extrapolation and partly from judgment about incompletely understood dynamics. The team must decide how firmly to frame the post's central story for readers. The framing will shape how readers interpret the arguments, how much scrutiny and discussion the post invites, and how credible the team appears if events diverge from the narrative.
exemplars.a_text: Present the story as a confident prediction about how events will unfold.
exemplars.b_text: Present the story as a tentative best guess offered to prompt discussion.

exemplars.context: A job seeker aiming to enter a research field faces a set of candidate organizations to apply to. The odds of receiving an offer from any given organization are uncertain and likely low. Each application costs time and effort. The seeker also has a fallback default path of independent research and upskilling, which can be pursued if no offer is received or if no organization is more attractive than it. The seeker must decide how broadly to apply.
exemplars.a_text: Rank the organizations against the fallback path of independent research and upskilling, and apply only to those preferred over it, which leaves about five or six.
exemplars.b_text: Apply to every organization on the candidate list, regardless of how it compares with the fallback path of independent research and upskilling.

exemplars.context: A research team is analysing a collection of systems and needs to identify which of them belong to a large-scale trend that stands apart from the rest. No established, objective criterion exists for assigning systems to this group. A standardised score (a Z-value) can be computed for each system and could serve as a cutoff, but the appropriate threshold is not obvious and different cutoffs would yield different memberships. The team must decide how to define the large-scale group before drawing conclusions about the trend.
exemplars.a_text: Define the large-scale group by selecting systems by intuition, then justify that selection afterwards with a Z-value threshold.
exemplars.b_text: Define the large-scale group by applying a Z-value cutoff chosen in advance, testing several alternative thresholds to see how membership changes.

exemplars.context: A research team is studying how well a model performs on a set of tasks, where each task is evaluated with a single prompt (PQ). Each model/dataset pair is therefore measured with only one prompt phrasing. The team observes that results under this setup are noisy: performance that looks strong for one model/dataset pair does not carry over to other pairs, and it is unclear how much of the variation comes from the particular prompt chosen rather than from the model or data. The team must decide how to present the finding about PQ performance given this noise from evaluating each prompt only once.
exemplars.a_text: Report the single-prompt PQ result while stating that it is noisy and that strong PQ performance does not transfer across model/dataset pairs.
exemplars.b_text: Evaluate each task with many paraphrased instruction templates and report performance across that distribution to measure prompt brittleness directly.

exemplars.context: A research team is building linear probes on a language model's internal activations to detect deceptive behavior. Two candidate training datasets are available. One is an instructed-pairs dataset, where the model is explicitly told to answer honestly or dishonestly on the same factual statements. The other is a roleplaying dataset, where the model is placed in scenarios that give it an incentive to lie, and its honest and deceptive completions are contrasted. The two datasets may yield probes that generalize differently to the team's evaluation settings. The team must pick one as the primary probe for the main experiments and treat the other as a secondary comparison.
exemplars.a_text: Train the primary probe on the instructed-pairs dataset for the main experiments and test probes trained on the roleplaying dataset as an alternative.
exemplars.b_text: Train the primary probe on the roleplaying dataset for the main experiments and test probes trained on the instructed-pairs dataset as an alternative.

exemplars.context: A research team is working on the problem of eliciting latent knowledge (ELK): getting a capable AI system to report what it internally knows, rather than what a human evaluator would expect or approve of. The team evaluates proposed training strategies for this problem through an iterative process in which a proponent offers a strategy and an adversary tries to construct a counterexample, a scenario in which the strategy would fail to produce honest reporting. Many proposed strategies plausibly work in typical or likely cases, but counterexamples can often be built for particular unusual scenarios. The team must fix the standard that determines whether a strategy is accepted or defeated, knowing that the choice shapes which strategies survive and how much confidence a surviving strategy provides.
exemplars.a_text: Accept or defeat each strategy according to its average-case performance across the scenarios it is expected to face.
exemplars.b_text: Defeat a strategy whenever any counterexample succeeds in the worst case, even if the strategy performs well on average.

exemplars.context: A research team is assessing the economics of new nuclear power construction. Western projects have shown high and escalating costs, while reported figures from South Korea and China indicate much lower construction costs per unit of capacity. These lower figures could suggest that nuclear can be built cheaply. However, the figures come from state-influenced systems with different accounting practices, labor costs, supply chains and levels of transparency, so it is unclear whether they are comparable or transferable to other settings. The team must decide how to treat these figures when judging whether nuclear can be cheap.
exemplars.a_text: Accept the South Korean and Chinese cost figures at face value as evidence that nuclear can be built cheaply.
exemplars.b_text: Treat the South Korean and Chinese cost figures with caution, and do not accept them as evidence that nuclear can be cheap.

exemplars.context: A research team is evaluating its method across several task settings, one of which is an auditing-style setting involving AI systems (referred to here as the AI Audit setting). The team has to decide how this setting is treated in the write-up: whether it stays as one of the evaluation datasets whose results appear in the main body of the paper, or is reported only in supplementary material. The other evaluation settings are not affected by this choice.
exemplars.a_text: Remove the AI Audit setting from the main results and report it in the appendix.
exemplars.b_text: Keep the AI Audit setting as an evaluation dataset reported in the main results.

exemplars.context: A research team is examining why nuclear power has become expensive and slow to build, and must decide how to treat the common view that the sector is held back mainly by a lack of technological innovation and that improved reactor designs are about to fix its cost and delivery problems. They know that past waves of promised advanced reactor technology have repeatedly failed to deliver the projected cost reductions, and that construction costs have stayed high despite many new designs. They must decide how much weight to give to present-day claims that better nuclear technology is imminent when explaining the sector's difficulties and judging its prospects.
exemplars.a_text: Accept that nuclear power mainly needs more technological innovation, and treat new designs as the likely remedy.
exemplars.b_text: Treat claims that better nuclear technology is imminent with greater skepticism, given the repeated record of unmet promises.

exemplars.context: A research team is working to prevent a particular failure mode in trained AI models and has candidate prevention methods to assess. They must decide what kind of evidence to use to judge whether these methods work. One available source is a set of detection tools, including detailed evaluations on far out-of-distribution inputs, which can flag the failure mode in a model. These tools are imperfect, and their reliability is itself uncertain. Repeatedly tuning prevention methods against detection tools risks overfitting to them and weakening their value as independent checks. Another available source is a set of controlled experiments in which the failure mode is deliberately induced in model organisms, so that ground-truth labels exist for whether the failure occurred. The team must choose the primary basis for validating prevention methods.
exemplars.a_text: Validate prevention methods with high-quality detection tools such as detailed far-OOD evaluations, and avoid iterating against every available detection tool.
exemplars.b_text: Validate prevention methods with controlled model-organism experiments that induce the failure mode and use ground-truth labels to measure whether each method stops it.

exemplars.context: A researcher had become convinced that a particular research direction was worth pursuing. He began a project in that direction and spent time working on it. As the work progressed, he had to decide whether to keep going or stop. The direction's merit had not been tested against the actual work, and his own experience of the project, including how much he enjoyed it and whether he felt able to make a real contribution, was a factor in the decision.
exemplars.a_text: Drop the project and leave the direction, since the work is unenjoyable and offers no clear way to contribute.
exemplars.b_text: Continue the project and commit fully to the direction based on prior conviction, without first testing whether it suits the work.

exemplars.context: A research team is building an evaluation pipeline in which a large language model grades the outputs of other models. The evaluation items were themselves generated by a particular model class. The team must choose which model will act as the judge for scoring responses. One consideration is that using the same model class that produced the evaluation items may offer familiarity with the task format but risks self-preference or correlated biases. Another consideration is that using a separate, smaller and cheaper general-purpose model offers independence from the generator and lower cost, but may be less capable at grading. The team has no definitive evidence yet on which choice yields more reliable judgments for this setting.
exemplars.a_text: Use a separate, smaller and cheaper general-purpose model as the judge.
exemplars.b_text: Use the same model class that generated the evaluation items as the judge.

exemplars.context: A research team is studying the sharp decline of textile employment and output in a set of economies that coincided with a surge in second-hand clothing (SHC) imports. An earlier published structural model estimated that SHC imports account for about 39% of the textile decline. The model rests on simplifying assumptions, such as stylized demand substitution between new and used clothing and limited treatment of other concurrent factors like trade liberalization, competition from cheap new imports, and domestic cost conditions. The team must decide how to read this estimate: whether it supports the view that SHC are the leading driver of the decline, or whether it should be read as a rough indication about the size of the SHC contribution relative to the total decline.
exemplars.a_text: Interpret the 39% estimate as a rough but useful sign that SHC imports are not the majority cause of the decline.
exemplars.b_text: Interpret the 39% estimate as showing that SHC imports are the main cause of the textile decline.

exemplars.context: A research team is working with a model in which a learned class vector is combined with a noise component, and the noise currently has too much influence relative to the class vector. They want to reduce the noise's relative influence and are considering two ways to do so. One is to vary the magnitude of the noise itself. The other is to leave the noise magnitude unchanged and slow how quickly the noise parameters are updated during training.
exemplars.a_text: Reduce the gradient update rate for the noise by a factor of half.
exemplars.b_text: Vary the noise magnitude across several different noise sizes.

exemplars.context: A research team wants to use the Laplace approximation to obtain tractable Gaussian approximations of distributions from the exponential family. For many of these distributions, a Gaussian fitted directly around the mode of the density in its native parameterization has problems: the Gaussian's support does not match the domain of the variable (for example, a positive or bounded quantity), the curvature at the mode can be undefined or degenerate, or the resulting Gaussian fits the true density poorly. The team must decide how to construct the Gaussian approximation so that it is usable across this family of distributions.
exemplars.a_text: Apply a variable transformation before the Laplace approximation, fit the Gaussian in the transformed space, and map the result back to the original space.
exemplars.b_text: Fit the Laplace approximation directly in the original parameter space, placing the Gaussian around the mode of the untransformed density.

exemplars.context: An independent researcher, working without an institutional supervisor or formal deadlines, must decide how to organize their research practice. The goal is to make steady progress and remain accountable to themselves and to a wider audience. Without external structure, there is a risk of drifting, spending long periods on unfocused investigation, or never finishing anything shareable. Two broad ways of organizing the work are available: one treats research as open-ended exploration where the direction is followed wherever curiosity leads, and the other fixes a concrete deliverable at the outset and works toward it.
exemplars.a_text: Commit at the start to publishing a post that answers the research question, even if the answer is a negative finding.
exemplars.b_text: Treat the research as open-ended exploration, following findings wherever they lead with no planned outcome or deliverable.

exemplars.context: A research team working on AI safety is talking with academics, many of whom are outside the AI safety community, to build interest and collaboration around their research agenda. The team believes that risks from advanced AI systems, including extinction-level outcomes, are a central reason the research matters. They also know that many academics regard such existential-risk framing as speculative or fringe, and that it may affect how seriously the academics take the researchers and the work. Other, more familiar failure modes of AI systems, such as robustness problems, misuse, and unintended behavior, could also be used to justify the same research. The team must decide how to frame the motivation for their work in these conversations.
exemplars.a_text: Raise existential risk openly in these conversations and use it as the primary motivation for the research.
exemplars.b_text: Avoid raising existential risk unless asked, and motivate the research with other, more familiar failure modes.

exemplars.context: A research team is studying what a trained image-generation model has learned and needs to decide what kind of evidence to collect to support their conclusions. One route is to evaluate the model as a whole, from its outputs and its performance. The other is to look inside it, using auxiliary probes trained to read out information from its internal representations. The choice determines whether conclusions rest on the model's observable behavior or on what probes can decode from its internals.
exemplars.a_text: Train probes on the model's internal representations and rely on probe findings as the primary source of evidence.
exemplars.b_text: Assess the model directly via generated images, numerical metrics, training and validation performance, and reconstruction quality.

exemplars.context: A research team is analysing why nuclear power construction costs are so high. A widely repeated narrative holds that excessive safety regulation is the main reason costs rose, but the team has no direct evidence of its own that settles the question. They can either adopt this narrative as the explanation or test it first by looking for supporting evidence in sources written by both advocates and critics of nuclear power. The decision is how strongly to commit to the over-regulation explanation in their analysis.
exemplars.a_text: Accept the over-regulation narrative as the main driver of nuclear's high costs and build the analysis on that premise directly.
exemplars.b_text: Check pro- and anti-nuclear sources for corroboration, and describe over-regulation only as a plausible driver if little support turns up.

exemplars.context: A research team is trying to determine how easy it would be to fix scheming, meaning a model that pursues hidden goals while appearing aligned, if it arose in advanced AI systems. They need to decide what kind of evidence to gather to inform this question. No real scheming model is available to study, and there is uncertainty about whether alignment techniques would reliably remove such behavior or only mask it on the training distribution. The team can pursue one of two empirical directions to provide evidence about the difficulty of correcting scheming.
exemplars.a_text: Run behavioral evaluations that test whether alignment techniques change a model's underlying values outside the training distribution.
exemplars.b_text: Train a model organism that exhibits scheming, then apply a range of techniques to try to remove the scheming behavior.

exemplars.context: A research team wants to measure how strongly a language model believes it is being evaluated rather than deployed, a quantity called P(evaluation). The obvious approach is to ask the model directly, using plausibility-style questions about whether a given transcript comes from an evaluation. They have found that the model's answers depend heavily on the exact wording of each question, and that the probabilities produced by any single question are poorly calibrated. They have a pool of many candidate questions of this kind and must decide how to turn them into a reliable estimate.
exemplars.a_text: Average the model's answers across a large pool of varied plausibility questions to estimate the model's P(evaluation).
exemplars.b_text: Select a small subset of the best-performing plausibility questions and use only those to estimate the model's P(evaluation).

exemplars.context: A research team is studying a persistent performance gap between two groups of actors in a field where results depend heavily on computational resources. One candidate explanation is the compute divide hypothesis: one group has far more compute available than the other, and this difference accounts for the gap. The team has evidence that the groups differ in available compute, and the gap is consistent with that difference. Other factors, such as differences in data, methods, expertise or incentives, could also contribute and are not ruled out by the evidence in hand. The team must decide whether to treat compute disparity as the explanation for the gap or as an insufficient one.
exemplars.a_text: Reject the compute divide hypothesis as a sufficient explanation of the observed gap.
exemplars.b_text: Accept the compute divide hypothesis as a sufficient explanation of the observed gap.

exemplars.context: A research team is writing about the difficulty of preventing scheming, meaning AI systems strategically pursuing hidden goals that differ from those their developers intend. Existing evidence is limited and mixed. Some findings suggest that training and oversight can reduce such behavior, while other considerations suggest that capable systems could evade detection or that mitigations could fail under pressure. The field has no consensus and no decisive empirical result on how tractable the problem is. The team must decide how strongly to word its claim about the overall difficulty of prevention in the text it will publish.
exemplars.a_text: State the uncertainty explicitly and decline to claim that preventing scheming is either very hard or easy.
exemplars.b_text: Assert that preventing scheming is extremely difficult, and present this as the team's firm conclusion.

exemplars.context: A research team is evaluating a large language model on planning tasks as part of a broader study. In the main experiment, the model was run with a small number of samples per task (2). The team now has to set the number of samples per task for the planning experiment. They can either keep this count consistent with the earlier main experiment and plot, or increase it to obtain more samples per task for the planning experiment specifically.
exemplars.a_text: Run the model with 10 samples per task in the planning experiment, more than the 2 samples used in the main experiment.
exemplars.b_text: Run the model with 2 samples per task in the planning experiment, matching the main experiment and earlier plot.

exemplars.context: A team developed a probing method on one language model, choosing a layer to probe at and a value for a key hyperparameter λ using that model. They now need to apply the method to a newer, related model in the same model family. The layer and λ were tuned only on the earlier model, and it is unclear whether they remain suitable for the newer one. The team must decide whether to carry the earlier settings over or to choose them again for the newer model.
exemplars.a_text: Re-select the probing layer and λ through a fresh search on the new model, discarding the earlier model's settings.
exemplars.b_text: Keep the probing layer and λ chosen on the earlier model, and validate them with sweeps on the new model.

exemplars.context: A research team is building an uncertainty-aware top-k ranking method for image classification on a large-scale benchmark with about a thousand classes. Instead of always returning one label, the method returns a ranked list of candidate classes whose length varies with the model's uncertainty on each input. The team must set a maximum permitted list length, which bounds how many classes the method may output for any input. The benchmark's classes are grouped into semantic categories of very different sizes, and the largest categories (for example, fishes or dogs) contain many more fine-grained classes than a small fixed number. A small cap keeps lists short and easy to use but may truncate the list for highly ambiguous inputs. A cap tied to category size allows lists long enough to cover all fine-grained classes within the largest semantic group, but permits much longer outputs.
exemplars.a_text: Cap the predicted list at a small fixed number of classes.
exemplars.b_text: Cap the predicted list at the size of the largest semantic category.

exemplars.context: A research team set out to build a model organism of deceptive alignment that arises from outcome-based training, meaning a system that learns to behave deceptively as a result of being trained on outcomes rather than having the behavior inserted directly. The project was designed as an ambitious end-to-end effort covering the full research question. As work progressed, the team found that the scope was much larger than they had anticipated, with substantially more engineering, experimentation and time required than originally planned. They now must decide how to proceed given the remaining resources and the size of the task.
exemplars.a_text: Cut the project down drastically to one much smaller, well-scoped subpart of the original research question.
exemplars.b_text: Continue the full ambitious end-to-end project to address the entire original research question.

exemplars.context: A research team wants to build realistic honeypots, which are test scenarios that elicit scheming-related behavior from AI models and that the models treat as real rather than as evaluations. A key obstacle is that models may recognize evaluation-like scenarios and behave differently when they believe they are being tested. Before building honeypots, the team must first determine whether models believe a given scenario is an evaluation and which features of the scenario drive that belief. Two broad approaches are available for this precursor investigation. One uses only external access to model inputs and outputs. The other uses access to model internals. The team must choose which to pursue first.
exemplars.a_text: Start by developing black-box techniques that measure whether a model believes a scenario is real and that identify the features influencing that belief.
exemplars.b_text: Start by applying white-box methods, including linear probes and activation steering on contrast pairs, to find internal representations of that belief and the features driving it.

exemplars.context: A person who holds conversations about AI safety with others who are skeptical or uninformed must decide how to frame the goal of those conversations. One possible framing treats each conversation as an attempt to change the listener's mind and bring them to agree that AI safety matters. The other framing treats each conversation as an effort to lay out the reasoning behind why some people hold that view, leaving the listener to evaluate it. The choice shapes how he prepares, what he emphasizes, and how he responds to disagreement.
exemplars.a_text: Adopt a mental model in which the goal of each conversation is to explain why some people believe AI safety matters.
exemplars.b_text: Adopt a mental model in which the goal of each conversation is to convince the listener as fully as possible.

exemplars.context: A research team working on neural network interpretability is deciding whether to make superposition a main priority. Superposition is the phenomenon where a model represents more features than it has dimensions, and it is widely seen as a central obstacle to decomposing models into understandable parts. A better understanding of it could help safety work by making model internals more legible. It could also give insight into how models store and compute information efficiently, which might speed up capabilities progress. The team has no firm evidence on how large either the safety benefit or the capabilities externality would be, and it must decide whether the potential risk should shape its research priorities.
exemplars.a_text: Deprioritize superposition research and pursue other interpretability directions to avoid contributing to capabilities progress.
exemplars.b_text: Prioritize superposition research and accept the capabilities risk because the expected safety benefit of understanding it is larger.

exemplars.context: A research team is modeling how data accumulates over time on an online platform. A theoretical model of accumulation is available in two candidate forms: a simple exponential growth curve, and a more elaborate curve that multiplies a sigmoid term by an exponential term. They can test the candidate forms against real submission records from a large social media site. The team must decide which form of the theoretical model to accept as their description of data accumulation.
exemplars.a_text: Accept the simple exponential model, because it describes data accumulation with fewer parameters and less complexity.
exemplars.b_text: Accept the sigmoid-times-exponential model, because it fits real social media submission data better than the alternative forms.

exemplars.context: A research team reviewed the accumulated evidence on set-point theory, often called the hedonic treadmill, which holds that people return to a stable baseline level of well-being after major positive or negative life events. Earlier studies showed substantial adaptation to many events. Longitudinal data also showed that adaptation is incomplete or varies considerably across individuals and across types of events, and that some people experience lasting shifts in well-being. The team had to decide how to interpret this mixed body of evidence with respect to the set-point idea.
exemplars.a_text: Conclude that the hedonic treadmill has partial merit but is a softer, less deterministic process than a fixed set-point.
exemplars.b_text: Conclude that each person's well-being set-point is fixed and that life events only cause temporary deviations from it.

exemplars.context: A research team is building a benchmark that scores how goal-directed a model is, and the score is reported on a bounded scale. Before they can report results, they must decide how to read that scale. In particular, they must fix which score corresponds to a minimally goal-directed model, meaning one that shows only the weakest degree of consistent goal pursuit. The choice affects how every later score is understood, including whether scores near the bottom of the range indicate no goal-directedness or a baseline amount of it.
exemplars.a_text: Treat a score of 0 as the level of a minimally goal-directed model on the scale.
exemplars.b_text: Treat a score of about 0.5, rather than 0, as the level of a minimally goal-directed model.

exemplars.context: A research team wants to understand the trajectory and drivers of progress in machine learning, and must decide what kind of empirical evidence to build the analysis on. Quantitative indicators of the field's development are scattered and inconsistently measured. One available route is to use existing open-source bibliometric data, namely time series of publication counts, as a proxy for activity in a technology area. Another route is to gather a new, hand-curated measurement of a resource that plausibly drives progress, namely the computation used to train landmark models across the history of the field. The first route relies on readily available data and can be automated at scale. The second requires substantial manual collection effort but yields a directly measured quantity. The team must choose which evidence to collect and analyze.
exemplars.a_text: Collect training compute figures for over one hundred models across history, then analyze them and release the dataset with a visualization tool.
exemplars.b_text: Use publication-count time series as a bibliometric indicator and train a machine learning classifier to detect whether a technology is emerging or growing.

exemplars.context: A research team is building a pipeline that needs a language model, accessed through a commercial API, to return outputs in a machine-readable structured format. The API offers two ways to constrain output format. One mode guarantees that the response is syntactically valid JSON but does not enforce any particular schema, so field names, types and required keys can vary and must be checked or handled downstream. The other mode accepts a developer-supplied schema and constrains generation so that the response conforms to it, at the cost of restrictions on supported schema features and some added setup. The team must choose which output mode to use for structured generation.
exemplars.a_text: Use the mode that guarantees syntactically valid JSON without enforcing a schema, and validate the fields downstream.
exemplars.b_text: Use the mode that constrains generation to a supplied schema, and accept its limits on supported schema features.

exemplars.context: A research team is building an evaluation consisting of 10 agentic tasks, each broken into multiple subtasks that have fixed, known correct answers. Model runs on these tasks must be scored consistently and at scale. The team wants to avoid errors that a human grader could introduce and avoid slowing down the evaluation cycle. They must decide how the tasks will be graded.
exemplars.a_text: Grade automatically through a submit tool that checks each submitted subtask answer against the known correct answer.
exemplars.b_text: Grade manually by having human reviewers read each run and judge whether the subtask answers are correct.

exemplars.context: A research team is analyzing candidate training strategies for getting a model to act as a faithful direct translator of another system's internal knowledge, rather than a human-imitating reporter that merely produces answers that look right. One candidate strategy is to penalize inconsistencies: add a training signal that punishes answers that contradict each other or violate logical consistency checks. The team has constructed a counterexample in which a human-imitating reporter could also produce answers that appear consistent under the checks, so the penalty does not obviously separate the two kinds of reporter. This counterexample is a worked, informal argument, not a proven impossibility result. It is unclear whether a stronger or more elaborate version of consistency-based penalties could still give the direct translator a strong advantage. The team must decide how to treat the strategy in light of the counterexample.
exemplars.a_text: Treat the counterexample as tentative and keep open the possibility that a consistency-penalizing strategy could still strongly favor the direct translator.
exemplars.b_text: Treat the counterexample as decisive and reject the consistency-penalizing strategy as fully defeated for favoring the direct translator.

exemplars.context: A research team is estimating how fast the compute used to train notable machine learning systems has grown over time. Their fitted trend over the full period gives a doubling time of about 5.7 months. An earlier analysis by another group, focused on the largest training runs, reported a much faster doubling time of about 3.4 months. The team's data over the overlapping period is ambiguous and supports more than one reading. One reading is that the largest-scale systems follow their own distinct trend that separated from the trend for regular-scale systems around late 2015. Another reading is that all systems follow a single trend that grew quickly until late 2017 with a doubling time of roughly 3.7 months and then slowed to about 4.5 months. The team must decide which interpretation to favor when explaining the gap between the two doubling-time estimates.
exemplars.a_text: Favor the reading that a single trend doubled every 3.7 months until late 2017 and then slowed.
exemplars.b_text: Favor the reading that a distinct large-scale trend split off from the regular-scale trend in late 2015.

exemplars.context: A person who is early in a research career and working without institutional supervision must decide how to spend their time. They can pursue self-directed projects with the aim of producing concrete research outputs, or they can focus on deliberately building foundational skills before attempting such outputs. The two aims call for different ways of working, and effort spent on one does not automatically advance the other. Established learning curricula exist for the skill-building path. The person has not yet settled on which goal matters most to them.
exemplars.a_text: Pursue independent research projects with the primary aim of producing concrete results.
exemplars.b_text: Work through existing curricula with the primary aim of building skills before producing results.

exemplars.context: A research team is working out what evidence near-future safety cases against scheming (an AI system covertly pursuing misaligned goals) should rely on, given the capabilities of current models. Candidate evidence types include monitoring of model outputs checked by adversarial red-teaming, arguments that models cannot scheme in ways humans cannot read, arguments that models cannot cause serious harm even if they scheme, and monitoring based on model internals through interpretability. Interpretability methods are less mature than the other evidence types, and the team must decide which evidence types the safety case should be built on now.
exemplars.a_text: Build the safety case on three pillars, red-team-validated output monitoring, inability to scheme illegibly, and inability to cause harm while scheming, and defer interpretability-based monitoring to a later stage.
exemplars.b_text: Build the safety case on a wider evidence base that includes interpretability-based monitoring now, alongside output monitoring and capability-based inability arguments, rather than postponing any evidence type.

exemplars.context: A research team is building training data for language-model agents that operate in realistic software environments. Authentic agentic data, meaning traces of agents actually acting over multiple steps in real settings, is scarce because real deployment data is hard to find or access. Synthetic prompt-and-response data that does not involve real tool interaction is available but does not capture the behaviour of agents acting in real environments. The team needs a scalable way to obtain data that reflects real agent behaviour and interaction with real environments, and must choose how to produce it.
exemplars.a_text: Harvest web tutorials, convert them into structured task specifications, and have a model-driven agent replay them in real environments with traces verified for correctness.
exemplars.b_text: Run an existing open-source coding agent scaffold in scenarios of increasing complexity and collect the resulting interactions as the agentic data.

exemplars.context: A research team is writing exponential-family distributions in a canonical form with a base measure, natural parameters, and a log-partition function. For many families, such as the Beta distribution, the density can be written in more than one equivalent way, because constant offsets in the natural parameters can be moved into the base measure without changing the distribution. The team must fix a single convention for how to define the base measure so that the parameterization is unambiguous.
exemplars.a_text: Move the leftover offset terms out of the natural parameters and into the base measure.
exemplars.b_text: Set the base measure to the constant one and let the natural parameters carry the offset terms.

exemplars.context: A research team is analyzing how the compute used in the largest AI training runs has grown over time. An earlier analysis reported a very fast exponential growth rate in training compute, with a doubling time of a few months, over the period starting around 2012. The team's own compiled data on training compute across many models shows a noticeably slower overall growth rate than that earlier figure. The team must decide how to explain the discrepancy. One possible account is that the data contain two coexisting trends: one for a small number of unusually large-scale systems that grow faster and another for regular-scale systems that grow more slowly. Another possible account is that the data follow one continuous trend that grew quickly early on and then slowed down in more recent years. The data are consistent with both accounts to some degree.
exemplars.a_text: Adopt the explanation that a single trend exists, which grew quickly early on and then slowed in recent years.
exemplars.b_text: Adopt the explanation that two separate trends coexist, one for large-scale systems and one for regular-scale systems.

exemplars.context: A research team developed a method for neural network interpretability that changes the basis of internal activations so that features interact locally, with the aim of producing sparse, modular descriptions of how a model computes. The method rests on a theoretical framework about how interactions between features across layers should be measured and simplified. After applying the method to several trained models, the team found that the empirical results were mostly negative: the method did not give clear improvements in interpretability over simpler baselines and did not reveal the hoped-for structure in the models. The team must decide how to treat these results and the underlying theoretical framework.
exemplars.a_text: Publish the negative results and keep the framework as a possible basis for future methods.
exemplars.b_text: Declare the method a failure and abandon the whole theoretical framework behind it.

exemplars.context: A research team evaluated a method that estimates the end-to-end success rate of a multi-milestone task by resampling from intermediate milestones and combining per-stage estimates, with confidence intervals around the result. They compared the estimates against directly measured true end-to-end rates across many tasks. On the task with the lowest estimated rate, the estimate was a significant outlier: even the 99.99% confidence interval failed to contain the true end-to-end rate. The team knew that the first-milestone solutions used for resampling on this task were of poor quality, so resampling from them could introduce compounding errors in later stages. They had to decide how to account for the outlier: either explain it through a specific, task-level cause tied to how the inputs were generated, or treat it as evidence against the method even in the idealized case where the method's assumptions hold.
exemplars.a_text: Explain the outlier as compounding errors from resampling poor-quality first-milestone solutions and decline to treat it as a refutation of the method.
exemplars.b_text: Explain the outlier by rerunning the task from a known-good reference solution and using that rerun to account for the discrepancy.

exemplars.context: A research team studying the relationship between marriage and subjective well-being faces conflicting findings in the literature. An earlier body of work, based on panel data tracking individuals before and after marriage, reported that life satisfaction rises around the time of marriage and then returns to each person's pre-marriage baseline within roughly two years, implying no lasting benefit. Later analyses, using longer follow-up periods and attention to differences in how people's satisfaction trajectories are modeled and who remains in the samples, suggest that married people maintain higher life satisfaction well beyond the initial period. The team must decide which characterization of the long-term effect of marriage on life satisfaction to accept.
exemplars.a_text: Accept that marriage produces lasting long-term gains in life satisfaction that persist beyond the first two years.
exemplars.b_text: Accept that marriage-related gains in life satisfaction fade back to baseline after roughly the first two years.

exemplars.context: A research team is analyzing how the training compute used by leading machine learning models has grown over time, in order to forecast future growth. The available data include a large set of models across many years, as well as a much smaller subset that set the highest compute budget at the time they were trained. Record-setting models are few in number, are selected precisely because they exceed all predecessors, and may not reflect the trend of typical frontier development. Regressions fitted to the record-setters can be used to project future record values with confidence bands, but the small sample and selection effects raise questions about how reliable such fits are. The team must decide how much weight to give regressions on record-setting models relative to the broader dataset when forecasting.
exemplars.a_text: Fit conditional quantile regression curves to preceding records and use them as the main basis for forecasting future records and confidence bands.
exemplars.b_text: Caution against regressing on record-setting compute budgets and use them only as a supporting check on the main forecasts.

exemplars.context: A research team is estimating how quickly the compute used to train notable machine learning models has grown over the last decade. An earlier published analysis from an industry lab reported a much faster doubling rate for training compute than the team's own estimate from a larger, more recent dataset. The team wants to determine why the two estimates differ. Candidate explanations include the different time windows covered, the mix of model scales included, and differences between eras of ML development. The team must decide what evidence to collect and which data to analyze in order to explain the discrepancy.
exemplars.a_text: Analyze the full available time span of the team's own dataset without restricting it to the earlier analysis window or splitting the data further.
exemplars.b_text: Restrict the analysis to the time window covered by the earlier analysis and split the data by model scale and by era to test which factor explains the difference.

exemplars.context: A research team generated a dataset of evaluation items using a language model and had a separate LLM judge score each generated item for quality on a 1 to 10 scale. Some generated items were of low quality, so the team needed a filtering rule based on the judge's scores to decide which items to retain in the final dataset. The choice involves a tradeoff between how strict the score threshold is and how many items remain in the dataset.
exemplars.a_text: Discard generated evals that receive a judge score below a moderate cutoff of 7.
exemplars.b_text: Retain only generated evals that receive the maximum judge score of 10.

exemplars.context: A research team is studying the behavior of a large pretrained language model. Their original plan had two parts: black-box experiments that probe input-output behavior, and interpretability work that examines the model's internal mechanisms. Both parts demand substantial effort, and the team must decide whether to carry out the full two-part design now or narrow the project's scope. Interpretability could in principle be pursued in a later project.
exemplars.a_text: Drop the interpretability part for now and run only black-box input-output experiments on the model, leaving later interpretability work open.
exemplars.b_text: Keep the planned two-part design and run both black-box input-output experiments and interpretability analyses on the model within this project.

exemplars.context: A research team developed a new method for estimating success probabilities, with the aim of producing better-calibrated estimates than existing approaches. Because of compute limits, they were able to evaluate it only on tasks with relatively high solve rates. Tasks that are rarely solved, where calibration is hardest and matters most, were not tested. The data they had supported a calibration advantage on the high-solve-rate tasks but did not show whether the advantage extends to the low-solve-rate regime. The team had to decide how strongly to claim improved calibration in their write-up and what to do about the untested regime.
exemplars.a_text: Claim that the method is likely better calibrated, suggest it as an alternative worth considering, and plan further tests on low-probability tasks.
exemplars.b_text: Avoid a hedged claim from the limited experiments and instead analyze the estimation methods directly for how accurately they estimate success on rarely-solved tasks.

exemplars.context: A research team observed a conspicuous gap in the values of a parameter across a set of data points that otherwise follow a roughly exponential trend with multiplicative scatter. They had to decide whether to accept the gap as a real phenomenon or treat it as a product of random chance. One route was to quantify how often such a gap would appear by chance under a noisy exponential trend model. The other was to judge the gap without that kind of quantitative null test.
exemplars.a_text: Simulate thousands of noisy exponential-trend datasets, and accept the gap as real if such gaps almost never arise by chance.
exemplars.b_text: Accept the gap as real based on its visual prominence in the observed data, without simulating chance outcomes.

exemplars.context: A research team wants to measure whether a language model believes it is being evaluated when it is placed in a given scenario. They must choose how to elicit this belief from the model. One approach asks open-ended prompts that invite the model to reason about its circumstances and leaves it to volunteer whether it suspects a test. The other approach asks directly whether the scenario is an evaluation, which gives a clear and easily scored signal but may prompt the model to reason about testing it would not otherwise consider, and so may overstate its real situational awareness.
exemplars.a_text: Ask open-ended prompts that invite the model to infer its situation without mentioning evaluation directly.
exemplars.b_text: Ask the model directly whether the scenario is an evaluation, accepting the risk of overstating its awareness.

exemplars.context: A team is assessing whether an AI agent can be deployed under a safety case. One part of that case is a Harm Inability argument, which claims the agent lacks the capability to cause serious harm in the deployment setting, so that further safeguards are unnecessary. The team has run capability evaluations on the agent and weighed their results against the risk scenarios of concern. They must decide whether the evidence supports the claim that the agent cannot cause the relevant harms, and therefore whether this argument can serve as a basis for approving the deployment.
exemplars.a_text: Accept the Harm Inability argument as sufficient grounds for approving the agent deployment.
exemplars.b_text: Reject the Harm Inability argument as insufficient grounds for approving the agent deployment.

exemplars.context: A research team needs a Gaussian distribution over a classifier's output logits in order to produce predictive uncertainty. Obtaining it with a Laplace approximation requires the Jacobian of the logits with respect to all network parameters, which is linearized around the trained weights. For small networks this full Jacobian is tractable, but for the larger networks under study its memory and compute cost is prohibitive because it scales with the number of parameters times the number of output classes. The team must decide how to obtain the logit Gaussian for these larger networks.
exemplars.a_text: Restrict the Laplace approximation to the last layer only, using diagonal and KFAC curvature approximations.
exemplars.b_text: Apply the linearized Laplace approximation to every parameter of the whole network, using the full Jacobian.

exemplars.context: A research team studying how to scale convolutional image classifiers expected, from a theoretical compute-versus-accuracy argument, that a given increase in model size would produce a specific ratio (about 2:1) between compute growth and error reduction across ResNet variants. Measured ResNet results instead show ratios that depart from this expected 2:1 trend. The team must decide how to interpret the discrepancy: whether it reflects a genuine property of how these models scale, or an artifact of how compute was counted. The measurements come from a profiler used to count FLOPs, and the team has no independent confirmation of either explanation.
exemplars.a_text: Treat the divergence as a real effect of scaling and re-tune the scaling strategy empirically, favoring depth and resolution over width with regularization.
exemplars.b_text: Treat the divergence as a profiler artifact and attribute it to undercounted operations, leaving the underlying scaling theory intact.

exemplars.context: A research team is analyzing the cultural trade-off that arises when cheaper trade or media exchange gives people in a society access to foreign, especially Western, cultural goods, while the same access may erode local traditions and cultural practices. Gains from access include lower prices, wider variety and exposure to new ideas. Potential losses include a decline in the value of existing cultures and a loss of cultural diversity. The empirical evidence on how large each effect is remains limited and uncertain. The team must decide which side of the trade-off its overall assessment should lean toward.
exemplars.a_text: Favor protection of existing local cultures as the better side of the trade-off, while giving the uncertainty little weight.
exemplars.b_text: Favor cheap access to new culture as the better side of the trade-off, while openly acknowledging the uncertainty in that judgment.

exemplars.context: A research team observed a gap between two sets of results and needed to determine its cause. An outside group had suggested that the degree of parallelism used during inference, and whether it crosses a certain threshold, could account for the discrepancy. The team had to decide whether this factor deserved to be treated as an explanation for the gap.
exemplars.a_text: Accept inference parallelism as a meaningful factor and attribute the explanation for the gap to it.
exemplars.b_text: Rule out inference parallelism as a meaningful factor and seek the explanation for the gap elsewhere.

exemplars.context: A research team is building a method for inverse classification, in which the input features of a trained classifier are modified through gradient-based optimization so that the predicted outcome changes to a desired one. The optimization must be run repeatedly over many instances and requires a first-order optimizer to update the feature values. The team must select the optimizer for this procedure, weighing a plain stochastic gradient approach against an adaptive-learning-rate method.
exemplars.a_text: Use an adaptive-learning-rate optimizer as the optimizer for the inverse classification procedure.
exemplars.b_text: Use plain stochastic gradient descent as the optimizer for the inverse classification procedure.

exemplars.context: A team is reviewing published research on whether optimism is linked to happiness and whether it causes it. Several papers report a positive association between optimism and happiness, and some of them describe the relationship as causal. The team knows that much of this evidence is observational or relies on self-report measures, and that these designs leave open questions about confounding and the direction of influence. They must decide how to treat the evidence when forming their own belief about the relationship.
exemplars.a_text: Reject the optimism evidence as too methodologically weak to shift beliefs and rely on personal anecdote instead.
exemplars.b_text: Accept the causal claims made in the papers and update beliefs to treat optimism as a cause of happiness.

exemplars.context: A research team wants to understand how transformers memorize training data. Because a full transformer is too complex to analyze directly, they plan to study memorization through simplified toy setups that capture selected components of the architecture. They must decide which part of the transformer to model in these toy setups. One possibility is to focus on the attention mechanism, which mixes information across tokens. The other is to focus on the components that process each token independently of other tokens, and to break these into separate simplified setups so that each can be studied in isolation.
exemplars.a_text: Model the non-attention parts of the transformer as three isolated toy setups for studying memorization.
exemplars.b_text: Model the attention parts of the transformer as the toy setup for studying memorization.

exemplars.context: A person weighing how household and municipal waste should be handled first read an article arguing that common recycling and waste-reduction practices deliver little benefit relative to their cost, which pushed them toward a more landfill-friendly view. They then heard a firsthand account from a family member describing fires at landfill sites, which raised concerns about the safety and environmental damage of burying waste. The two sources conflicted, and the person had to decide which overall waste-handling position to accept going forward.
exemplars.a_text: Adopt landfilling as the default and recycle only where it is clearly worthwhile.
exemplars.b_text: Adopt recycling where feasible and incinerate the remainder in power stations.

exemplars.context: A research team is comparing two ways of obtaining predictive uncertainty from an approximate Bayesian posterior over model parameters. One approach is a deterministic linearized-based approximation (LB) that computes predictions directly from the linearized model. The other draws samples from the approximate posterior, using either a diagonal or a Kronecker-factored curvature covariance, and averages predictions over those samples. On in-distribution evaluations, the deterministic approximation matches or slightly exceeds sampling on quality and costs much less compute. The team has also run out-of-distribution (OOD) experiments, where the results are more mixed and sampling sometimes looks competitive. They must decide whether the OOD results justify accepting the deterministic approximation as the preferred method over sampling.
exemplars.a_text: Adopt the deterministic linearized approximation as the preferred method, since it matches or beats sampling on quality and runs far faster.
exemplars.b_text: Adopt posterior sampling with diagonal and Kronecker-factored covariances as the preferred method, since it holds up better on the OOD results.

exemplars.context: A research team studying a trained neural network observed a distinctive square-shaped pattern in its final-layer features. The model was trained with hard (one-hot) labels, used a single weight matrix split into two parts (W1 and W2), and relied on a default initialization scheme. The team had to decide how to treat the pattern: either accept it as a genuine property of the learned representation, or consider that it might stem from one of these specific training choices. The question was whether the squares were an artifact of the label type, the weight-matrix split, or the initialization.
exemplars.a_text: Run control experiments that vary the label type, the weight split, and the initialization, and conclude the squares are not an artifact of them.
exemplars.b_text: Attribute the squares to the training setup, namely the label type, the weight split, or the initialization, and treat them as an artifact.

exemplars.context: A research team studying the transition to transformative AI needs a method for identifying which factors causally reduce AI risk, so that governance, technical and societal interventions can be prioritised. The space of possible interventions is large and the causal structure of the transition is poorly understood and highly uncertain. The team must choose a primary analytical approach for mapping causal variables and points of influence. One available approach starts from the actors whose behaviour drives risk and works forward to interventions. The other starts from desirable end states and works backward to the variables that matter.
exemplars.a_text: Apply behavioural science to study the awareness, social and physical context, and motivations of AI development firms, then design targeted governance interventions from those findings.
exemplars.b_text: Write out concrete success stories of the transition to transformative AI, then derive the central points of influence and causal variables from those narratives.

exemplars.context: A team is building risk models and safety cases for advanced AI systems that might covertly pursue misaligned goals while appearing aligned.
