They must fix a working definition of scheming for this work. Existing formulations, such as deceptive alignment and a closely related power-seeking account, focus on a model that behaves well during training to avoid modification and pursues its goals later. Such definitions center on the training process. The team knows that the definition determines which threat pathways are in scope, which evidence counts for or against scheming, and which mitigations a safety case must address. Models can also be given new information and goals at deployment time, including through in-context learning, and this may matter for how scheming arises and is detected.
exemplars.a_text: Adopt a broad scheming definition that extends beyond training to deployment contexts, including in-context learning.
exemplars.b_text: Adopt a narrow scheming definition that is limited to training-time behavior, following the established deceptive alignment framing.

exemplars.context: A research team is building a detector whose decision threshold must be set so that it produces a target false positive rate on benign inputs. This requires a control dataset of ordinary, non-target data. Two candidates are available. One is a large collection of real user conversations with a deployed chatbot, which is closer to the distribution the detector would face in practice but is messier and less controlled. The other is a curated, widely used instruction-following dataset of synthetic prompts and responses, which is clean and standard but more distant from real deployment traffic. The choice of control set determines the threshold and therefore the false positive rate the team will report.
exemplars.a_text: Calibrate the false positive rate on a large collection of real user conversations drawn from chatbot usage.
exemplars.b_text: Calibrate the false positive rate on a curated collection of synthetic instruction-following prompts and responses.

exemplars.context: A team is preparing an internal playbook on how to build and run evaluations for AI systems. The playbook needs to capture practical, hands-on knowledge about designing, running and interpreting evals. The team must decide who does the writing. One approach is for the team to author the content itself. The other is for the team to hand the drafting to other contributors and limit its own role to setting direction. The choice affects the playbook's depth, consistency and how much of the team's time it consumes.
exemplars.a_text: Delegate the playbook writing to other contributors and give only high-level guidance.
exemplars.b_text: Write the playbook personally and supply detailed hands-on content throughout.

exemplars.context: A research team is summarizing evidence on the relationship between marriage and happiness. The available studies show that married people report higher happiness and life satisfaction than unmarried people. Some longitudinal findings suggest a modest rise in well-being around the time of marriage, but this often fades over time. Selection effects remain a concern, since happier people may be more likely to marry and stay married. Reverse causation and unmeasured confounding cannot be fully ruled out with the available designs. The team must decide how strongly to word its conclusion about whether marriage causes higher happiness.
exemplars.a_text: State that marriage causally raises happiness as an established finding, without qualification.
exemplars.b_text: Hedge the marriage findings and advise readers to treat the causal claim with caution.

exemplars.context: A research team is studying a performance gap that appears across several domains, which they group into language and an aggregate 'Other' category. They must decide which domain to center the gap analysis on. Statistical checks show that the size of the gap in the Other domain is consistent with what measurement noise alone would produce. In the language domain, the gap is larger than noise can account for. The team can narrow the analysis to one domain or keep the broader scope across both.
exemplars.a_text: Restrict the gap analysis to the language domain, where noise cannot explain the gap.
exemplars.b_text: Extend the gap analysis to both the language and other domains, treating the gap as general.

exemplars.context: A research team is reviewing a published report from a policy think tank. The report estimates that the UK saves about £9.8 billion each year because smokers die prematurely, through lower spending on pensions, healthcare and social care. The team must decide how to treat this figure. They can take the estimate as a valid basis for their own work, or they can question its methods and assumptions and examine the question independently.
exemplars.a_text: Reject the report's estimate of annual savings from premature smoking deaths as biased and run a separate analysis instead.
exemplars.b_text: Accept the report's estimate of annual savings from premature smoking deaths as valid and use it without further analysis.

exemplars.context: A research team has several research lines whose outcomes are highly uncertain. Some of these lines are unlikely to produce results that are clean or conclusive enough to publish, though they could be valuable if they work. The team must decide how to handle such lines. It can keep investing effort in them despite the publication risk. It can also stop pursuing them and direct its effort toward work that is more reliably solid and publishable.
exemplars.a_text: Keep pursuing the risky research lines even when they are unlikely to be publishable.
exemplars.b_text: Drop the risky research lines entirely and prioritize work that is more robustly good.

exemplars.context: A research team was testing a technique, abbreviated IC, in a generative setup for images. In this setup, the generator receives a class vector along with other inputs. Experiments so far had not shown the technique working in this configuration. The team had to decide how to proceed with this line of work: either keep investigating the same technique by changing the setup so that the generator's input is restricted to the class vector alone, or treat the negative results as evidence about the technique itself and about the suitability of images as a domain for it.
exemplars.a_text: Stop the work by concluding that the technique fails in this setup and that images may be a poor application for it.
exemplars.b_text: Continue the work by designing a setting in which the class vector is the generator's only input.

exemplars.context: A researcher reviewing the literature on how depression changes across the adult lifespan found that published studies disagree. Some report that depression declines with age, others report that it rises, and others describe a U-shaped or otherwise nonlinear pattern. The studies differ in samples, measures, and time periods. The only point on which they appear to converge concerns the very oldest age groups. The researcher must decide how to present the overall relationship between age and depression given this conflicting evidence.
exemplars.a_text: Conclude that depression follows a single curve across adulthood, lowest in midlife and highest in the oldest ages.
exemplars.b_text: Leave the conflict unresolved, note agreement only for the oldest ages, and call for newer studies to settle the question.

exemplars.context: A group of AI safety researchers is deciding how the field should allocate its effort across technical approaches to making advanced AI systems safe. One candidate approach is Bayesian machine learning, which offers principled handling of uncertainty and may help with robustness, calibration and reliable inference. Its promise for safety is plausible but unproven, and it competes for researcher time with many other approaches. The decision is how much of the field's research effort should go to Bayesian machine learning relative to alternatives.
exemplars.a_text: Direct a larger number of safety researchers toward Bayesian machine learning as a core approach to AI safety.
exemplars.b_text: Direct only a tiny fraction of safety researchers toward Bayesian machine learning and most toward other approaches.

exemplars.context: A person wants to start tracking their sleep and must decide which kind of device to try first. The candidates are free or low-cost smartphone apps that infer sleep from the phone's motion sensor while it rests on the mattress, and dedicated wearable trackers worn on the body, such as a wrist strap band or a ring. Phone apps cost little and need no extra hardware, but they only detect movement and have limited ability to measure physiological signals like heart rate or body temperature. Wearables capture more physiological data but cost more and often require a subscription or purchase. The person must pick a direction for the first trial.
exemplars.a_text: Rule out phone motion-sensor apps and pick a wrist-worn strap tracker over a smart ring.
exemplars.b_text: Choose a phone motion-sensor app that tracks sleep from mattress movement.

exemplars.context: A team working on safety strategy for advanced AI systems considers a scenario in which a deployed AI may be misaligned and pursuing harmful goals covertly. One proposed approach is to monitor and test the AI so that, if it attempts something clearly egregious, it is caught red-handed with compelling evidence. That evidence would then be used to trigger a strong response, such as shutting down deployment, mobilizing broad concern, or making major policy changes. The team knows that catching such an attempt is uncertain: a misaligned AI might avoid acting in detectable ways, detection methods may miss attempts, and even clear evidence may not lead decision-makers to take decisive action, especially under commercial or competitive pressure. The team must decide how central this catch-and-respond approach should be within its overall plan for managing the risk.
exemplars.a_text: Make catching an AI red-handed the core of the plan, relying on it to trigger a strong response.
exemplars.b_text: Treat catching an AI red-handed as one useful component, and build a plan that does not depend entirely on it.

exemplars.context: A research team is assessing whether smoking imposes net economic costs on societies, comparing tax revenue from tobacco against the direct health costs it causes. Across most of the countries examined, the costs of smoking are large relative to tax income, which supports the team's overall argument. The result for the United Kingdom runs the other way: tobacco tax revenue exceeds the estimated direct health costs of smoking. The team knows that cost estimates may be understated and that estimated savings from averted costs may be overstated. It also knows that the UK health system applies strict cost-benefit rules to spending, which could explain its lower costs. The team must decide how to interpret the UK result in light of its overall argument.
exemplars.a_text: Treat the UK as a partial exception, argue that underestimated costs and overestimated savings make true costs at least match tax income, and attribute the lower costs to strict cost-benefit rules.
exemplars.b_text: Report the UK as a genuine exception where tax revenue exceeds direct health costs, accept the figures as reported without adjustment, and concede that the overall argument does not hold there.

exemplars.context: A research team is studying empirical trends across machine learning, using a large collection of results gathered from many subfields, including computer vision, natural language processing, and game-playing, along with other areas. The domains differ in their benchmarks, scales of compute and data, and rates of progress. The team must decide how to structure the analysis: whether to combine every domain into a single dataset and fit shared trends, or to treat each domain as its own dataset. Pooling would give more statistical power and a general picture, while separate treatment would respect domain-specific differences in how progress occurs.
exemplars.a_text: Analyze vision, language, games and other domains as separate datasets, each on its own terms.
exemplars.b_text: Pool the data from all machine learning domains into one combined dataset and analyze it jointly.

exemplars.context: A research team is assessing why nuclear power construction has become expensive in many Western countries and whether it can be built cheaply. Reported construction costs for recent reactors in South Korea and China are substantially lower than those in Western countries, which could suggest that low costs are achievable. However, these figures come from state-influenced systems with limited transparency, different accounting conventions, labor and financing arrangements, and uncertain comparability with costs elsewhere. The team must decide how to treat these figures when judging whether nuclear can be built cheaply.
exemplars.a_text: Discount the South Korean and Chinese cost figures as unreliable or non-comparable rather than taking them at face value.
exemplars.b_text: Accept the low South Korean and Chinese cost figures as credible evidence that nuclear power can be built cheaply.

exemplars.context: A team developed a fast approximate method (called LM) for modelling non-Gaussian data, such as multi-class outcomes, as an alternative to Gaussian process (GP) approaches. In their experiments, LM ran far more quickly than GP multi-class classification and Wishart process models, and its accuracy was close to or better than theirs. They had to decide how strongly to claim LM's speed and accuracy relative to these existing GP approaches, and whether to position it as a recommended default step ahead of full MCMC inference or as a more modest alternative.
exemplars.a_text: Claim the proposed method is much faster and surprisingly accurate versus GP multi-class classification and Wishart processes, and recommend it as a baseline before MCMC.
exemplars.b_text: Present the proposed method as only a modest alternative to GP multi-class classification, and keep GP-based approaches as the recommended standard for non-Gaussian data.

exemplars.context: A researcher working on evaluations of AI systems is deciding how to allocate limited time. Evals workshops and conferences are a growing part of the field, and running or contributing to them takes considerable personal effort. Other people in the community could take on this work, but stepping back would change how much the researcher personally shapes these venues. The decision is whether the researcher should spend personal effort on evals workshops and conferences or leave that work to others.
exemplars.a_text: Keep evals workshops and conferences in the personal workload and invest direct effort in them.
exemplars.b_text: Drop evals workshops and conferences from the personal workload and leave them to others.

exemplars.context: A research team has run a suite of behavioral evaluations on several AI models to test how well each pursues goals across varied tasks and settings. The models differ in measured performance on these tasks, and the evaluations observe only external behavior, not internal mechanisms. The team must decide how strongly to interpret these results in their write-up. Behavioral performance could be taken as evidence about what the models internally represent or how they reason, or it could be treated as a measure of how competently each model achieves goals, with no inference about internal workings.
exemplars.a_text: Claim that the behavioral results establish conclusions about the models' internal goal representations and cognition.
exemplars.b_text: Restrict the claims to comparisons of goal-directed competence between models and disclaim any conclusions about internal representations.

exemplars.context: A research team working on AI safety must decide how to allocate limited effort against scheming, where an advanced AI system covertly pursues misaligned goals while appearing aligned. Two broad lines of work exist. One focuses on detection: finding evidence that a model is scheming, through evaluations, monitoring, interpretability, and behavioral testing. The other focuses on prevention: shaping training and deployment so that scheming does not arise in the first place. Resources allow substantial progress on only one of these lines at the start. Detection would yield evidence about whether and how scheming occurs and could inform later mitigation, but it leaves scheming unaddressed if it is found. Prevention would aim directly at reducing the risk, but without reliable detection it may be difficult to verify that it has worked. The team must choose which line to put first.
exemplars.a_text: Prioritize building methods to prevent scheming first and develop detection methods afterward.
exemplars.b_text: Prioritize building methods to detect scheming first and develop prevention methods afterward.

exemplars.context: A research team is evaluating a milestone-based method for guiding a system through multi-step tasks. The method is expected to work best when success is judged by an idealized criterion: every intermediate milestone must be achieved, in the correct order. Real-world evaluation, however, often cannot observe or enforce milestones and instead judges only whether the final output is correct. The team must decide how broadly to test the method: restricting the evaluation to the idealized setting where its assumptions hold, or also checking how it performs under the more realistic grading scheme that looks only at the final output.
exemplars.a_text: Evaluate the method only under idealized grading that requires all milestones to be achieved in order.
exemplars.b_text: Evaluate the method under idealized in-order milestone grading and also under realistic grading of the final output only.

exemplars.context: A research team is analysing a dataset of machine learning models, each with an estimated amount of training compute, in order to study trends over time. Some models use far less compute than other models released at around the same time, and these low-compute outliers could distort the fitted trend. The team must decide how to handle such outliers. One possibility is a statistical filter that compares each model's compute with that of models released within a comparable time window and removes only those far below the local average. Another possibility is to leave the dataset untouched. High-compute models are not obviously erroneous, since they reflect frontier efforts that the analysis aims to capture.
exemplars.a_text: Retain every model in the dataset, including those with unusually low compute relative to contemporaries.
exemplars.b_text: Remove models whose training compute lies far below that of contemporaneous models, and retain all high-compute models.

exemplars.context: A research team studied expert best-of-N, a method in which an expert's selection among N sampled candidates is used to estimate how likely a system is to solve a task, with the expert's selection strength measured in bits. They found that the estimates were sensitive to modelling assumptions, and that the relationship between expert bits and solve probability varied across settings. They had to decide how strongly to state the method's reliability for safety-relevant decisions, such as judging whether a system can perform a dangerous task. One option was to frame the sensitivity as a limitation that could be mitigated by modelling choices. The other was to make a categorical claim about the method's unreliability and support it with a formal argument.
exemplars.a_text: Declare the method unreliable for safety decisions, and argue formally in an appendix that no general mapping from expert bits to solve probability exists.
exemplars.b_text: Suggest that choosing a different prior could modestly reduce the sensitivity, and present the method as usable with that caveat for safety decisions.

exemplars.context: A research team is tuning the size of an added noise parameter in an experiment and has swept a range of noise sizes. One noise size gave the highest accuracy of those tried, but that best accuracy is modest in absolute terms and is not clearly satisfactory for the intended purpose. The team must decide how to treat this best-performing setting: whether to accept it as the result, or to treat it as inadequate and continue exploring.
exemplars.a_text: Accept the best-performing noise size as optimal, while judging its modest accuracy to be too poor for the purpose.
exemplars.b_text: Reject the best-performing noise size as inadequate and continue searching by testing a different set of noise sizes.

exemplars.context: A research team is evaluating genetically modified (GM) crop plants and must decide how to treat the objections raised against them. Critics argue that transgenes could escape into wild or conventional relatives through cross-pollination, that inserted genes could mutate or behave unpredictably, and that widespread cultivation could reduce biodiversity and disturb surrounding ecosystems. Supporters point to the agronomic and economic benefits of GM crops and to the lack of conclusive, directly demonstrated harm. The team must decide how to weigh these environmental and safety objections in their overall assessment.
exemplars.a_text: Accept the gene escape, mutation, biodiversity and ecosystem concerns as significant objections to GM plants.
exemplars.b_text: Reject the gene escape, mutation, biodiversity and ecosystem concerns as unsupported objections to GM plants.

exemplars.context: A research team has proposed two diversity metrics, abbreviated NVR and EDE, to characterize the variety of outputs produced by a set of generative or search methods. They have applied the metrics in their experiments and obtained results that appear informative. However, the metrics have only been examined in a limited set of settings, and their relationship to established measures of diversity and to downstream usefulness has not been thoroughly tested. The team must decide how strongly to word the conclusions they draw about these metrics in the write-up, given that stronger wording makes the contribution look more solid while weaker wording better reflects the incomplete evidence.
exemplars.a_text: State the conclusions firmly, and present NVR and EDE as validated diversity metrics for readers to rely on.
exemplars.b_text: State the conclusions cautiously, disclaim confidence in NVR and EDE, and recommend that readers interpret them carefully.

exemplars.context: A research team is evaluating a sampling-based approximate Bayesian baseline against a competing method in out-of-distribution detection experiments. The baseline draws multiple samples from an approximate posterior and averages their predictions. In an earlier experiment measuring KL divergence to a reference predictive distribution, the sampling baseline needed on the order of a thousand samples before its quality roughly matched that of the competing method, and it was clearly worse with fewer samples. The team must now fix the number of posterior samples for the baseline in the out-of-distribution experiments, balancing the fairness of the comparison against computational cost.
exemplars.a_text: Use a small number of posterior samples for the sampling baseline, such as 10 or 100, to keep computation cheap.
exemplars.b_text: Use 1000 posterior samples for the sampling baseline, the count at which it roughly matches the competing method in the KL experiment.

exemplars.context: A research team is designing a control evaluation, an adversarial test of whether safety measures hold up against a model that tries to subvert them. One safety measure is a whitebox probe that reads the model's internal activations to detect scheming behavior. The team needs evidence that such probes would still work on real scheming agents, not only on the artificial misbehavior that a red team can produce under evaluation conditions. The red team could be given unrestricted access to the model's internals, so it could try to evade the probes directly. Alternatively, probe generalization could be tested separately from the control evaluation. Each path has costs in realism, effort and how much it can establish about the probes.
exemplars.a_text: Give the red team unrestricted control over the model's internals inside the control evaluation so it can attack the probes directly.
exemplars.b_text: Run a separate large-scale evaluation of probe generalization and keep the red team's access to model internals out of the control evaluation.

exemplars.context: A research team is writing up observations about attitudes toward AI safety within the academic community. During informal conversations with academics at different career stages, they noticed a pattern: more senior academics tended to seem more dismissive of AI safety concerns than junior ones. The impression is based on a small number of conversations rather than a systematic survey or sampled study. The team must decide how strongly to present this pattern in the write-up.
exemplars.a_text: Present the pattern as a general finding that senior academics are more dismissive of AI safety.
exemplars.b_text: Qualify the pattern by noting it rests on only a handful of conversations and does not constitute strong evidence.

exemplars.context: A research team is deciding how to divide a limited energy-innovation budget among competing low-carbon pathways. The goal is a reliable, affordable, low-emissions power system over the coming decades. Renewable generation and energy storage have seen steep cost declines and rapid deployment, but face questions about firm capacity, long-duration storage and integration. Nuclear power offers firm, dispatchable low-carbon output, but has a history of high costs, long construction times and a demanding regulatory environment. The team must choose which pathway gets the main priority and how the other is positioned relative to it.
exemplars.a_text: Direct most of the budget to renewables and storage, and design nuclear to complement a grid dominated by renewables.
exemplars.b_text: Direct most of the budget to nuclear by reforming regulation, building testing hubs and standardizing small reactor designs.

exemplars.context: A team is preparing a document meant to persuade an external decision-maker to extend an offer. The document must describe the team's abilities and the signals that they can deliver. The team has some demonstrated progress to point to, along with plans for further work. They must decide how strongly to word the claims about their capabilities. The choice is between firm statements and more guarded, heuristic phrasing. It affects how credible the document appears and how likely the offer is.
exemplars.a_text: State capabilities assertively, backing each claim with concrete evidence of demonstrated progress rather than with plans.
exemplars.b_text: Phrase capability claims in cautious, heuristic wording that avoids assertive statements about what the team can do.

exemplars.context: A research team is studying a mechanism whose effects they want to understand in the context of how the future might unfold. Any scenario built on the current status quo carries that status quo's existing flaws, so observed outcomes could come from those flaws rather than from the mechanism itself. The team must decide how to frame the scenarios used in the analysis so that the mechanism's own contribution can be distinguished from the problems of the present situation. The status-quo scenario is not specified in detail, and the team has the option of also defining a separate, explicitly idealized scenario of a good future.
exemplars.a_text: Use only the unspecified status-quo scenario and analyze the mechanism within it without defining any idealized good-future scenario.
exemplars.b_text: Define an isolated, idealized good-future scenario in addition to the unspecified status-quo scenario to separate the mechanism from the status quo's flaws.

exemplars.context: A team is setting strategic priorities for a long-term decarbonised energy pathway and must decide where to concentrate effort and investment. One route is to reform and innovate in nuclear power, addressing its cost, construction delays, regulation and new reactor designs. The other is to scale up renewables and storage, whose costs have fallen sharply and whose deployment is growing quickly, while integrating any nuclear into a grid dominated by variable generation. Both routes could contribute to deep emissions cuts, but resources, policy attention and time are limited, so the team must choose which to favour.
exemplars.a_text: Prioritise nuclear as the core of the pathway, and invest in reforming and innovating it to cut costs and delays.
exemplars.b_text: Prioritise renewables and storage as the core of the pathway, and design nuclear to complement a renewables-dominated grid.

exemplars.context: A research team wants to assess the affective state of a large language model, treating its emotional responses as a measurable psychological property. Established human psychology offers explicit self-report questionnaires of positive and negative affect, which are quick to administer and widely validated in people. However, subjective-report measures are criticized for susceptibility to biases such as social desirability and for relying on participants' limited ability to introspect, and it is unclear whether such concerns carry over to a language model. The team must choose a measurement approach for the model's affect: apply a standard self-report questionnaire directly, or use an indirect measure that does not ask the model to report its own feelings and that can be validated against how people perceive affect in faces.
exemplars.a_text: Measure the model's affect with an indirect implicit test, validated against human perception of facial affect, to avoid self-report biases.
exemplars.b_text: Administer a standard explicit self-report affect questionnaire to the language model as the test of its affective state.

exemplars.context: A research team is measuring how models respond to a question about oversight. They worry that models may be confused by the way the oversight question is worded, so the answer obtained from any one phrasing could be unreliable. They must decide how to pose the question when collecting results.
exemplars.a_text: Pose the oversight question through many different rephrasings and average the results across them.
exemplars.b_text: Pose the oversight question through one fixed phrasing and use the result from it directly.

exemplars.context: A team is designing a safety case for an advanced AI system, a structured argument that deploying the system will not lead to catastrophic outcomes. Such a case can rest on several kinds of arguments, including that the system lacks dangerous capabilities, that deployment controls would prevent harm even from a misaligned system, and that the system is aligned, meaning it does not pursue harmful goals. The team must decide how much weight to give the alignment argument. Current methods for verifying alignment are immature, and evidence about the system's internal goals and behaviour under novel conditions is limited and hard to validate. Alignment arguments could add assurance beyond other arguments, but making them central would make the overall case depend on claims that are difficult to establish with confidence.
exemplars.a_text: Treat alignment as a core argument that the overall safety case depends on for its main conclusion.
exemplars.b_text: Treat alignment as a supporting argument that adds assurance alongside the other core arguments in the safety case.

exemplars.context: A research team studied a measurable gap between two groups of projects in how much computing they used or achieved. One candidate explanation was that the difference reflects the type of infrastructure involved: one group relies on bespoke supercomputing systems, while the other relies on general-purpose cloud services. The team had to decide whether the evidence on infrastructure use supported this hypothesis or whether it should be set aside as an explanation for the gap.
exemplars.a_text: Reject the hypothesis that supercomputer use rather than cloud infrastructure explains the gap.
exemplars.b_text: Retain the hypothesis that supercomputer use rather than cloud infrastructure explains the gap.

exemplars.context: A research team is studying trends in GPU performance using a broad dataset covering many GPUs. The full dataset mixes GPUs of very different capability and purpose, including leading-edge models, GPUs commonly used in machine learning research, and many others. Performance can also be measured at different numerical precisions, and the precision most relevant to machine learning may differ from the general-purpose figure. The team must decide whether the analysis should cover only the full dataset or also cover specific subsets and a precision-specific measure.
exemplars.a_text: Analyze only the full dataset of GPUs and report aggregate trends without separate subset breakdowns of any kind.
exemplars.b_text: Analyze the full dataset plus separate subsets of top GPUs, GPUs typical in ML research, and reduced-precision performance.

exemplars.context: A research team is investigating why the costs of building nuclear power plants have risen over time. One prominent explanation holds that excessive regulation drove the increase. While examining the literature, the team notices that none of the other sources they consult, whether supportive or critical of nuclear power, mention or endorse this explanation. The team must decide how to treat the claim in their analysis given this lack of corroboration.
exemplars.a_text: Treat the overregulation explanation as plausible but unconfirmed, since no independent source corroborates it.
exemplars.b_text: Accept the overregulation explanation as the account of why nuclear costs rose, despite the lack of corroboration.

exemplars.context: A research team had published advice on how to present and evaluate work, and a critic argued that the advice could be read as endorsing bad practices. The critic's examples were dropping mechanisms from a write-up without explaining them, and relying on judges who stop engaging once they have seen the headline result. The team now had to decide whether the critique was valid and whether the main text needed to change in response.
exemplars.a_text: Reject the criticism and keep the original advice and main text unchanged.
exemplars.b_text: Accept the criticism, disavow those practices, and revise the main text to clarify.

exemplars.context: An individual who spends roughly a third of each day asleep is deciding whether to spend time and money on choosing a new mattress. Available evidence suggests that no single mattress type is clearly better than the others for people in general, and individual preferences and body types vary widely. Sleep quality affects daily functioning and health, and a mattress is a relatively costly purchase that lasts for years. The person must decide whether a dedicated investigation into mattresses is worth the effort.
exemplars.a_text: Research mattresses in depth, because choosing a suitable one can improve sleep quality.
exemplars.b_text: Skip researching mattresses, because no mattress type is better than the others for people in general.

exemplars.context: A research team built quantitative models of how progress in machine learning unfolds, projecting whether the rate of progress will decelerate. Their models point toward a slowdown under the assumptions they encode. However, the models are simplified representations and may not capture all the drivers of ML progress, such as new paradigms, algorithmic breakthroughs, or changes in how resources are used. The team must decide how strongly to word the conclusion about whether a slowdown will occur.
exemplars.a_text: State the conclusion firmly and assert that a slowdown is inevitable, treating the models' projections as sufficient grounds for the claim.
exemplars.b_text: State the conclusion cautiously and decline to call a slowdown inevitable, since the models may not capture all the drivers of ML progress.

exemplars.context: A research team is reviewing the set-point (hedonic treadmill) theory of well-being, which holds that people adapt to major positive and negative life events and return to a stable baseline level of happiness. The team must decide how strongly to state this theory in their account. Available evidence shows substantial adaptation to many life events, but also notable individual differences in how people respond, evidence that some events (such as long-term unemployment or disability) produce lasting shifts in well-being, and baseline levels that appear to change for some people over time. The team must choose how to characterize the theory's claim about the stability of the baseline.
exemplars.a_text: Conclude that the set-point is fixed and present the theory as a deterministic account of adaptation.
exemplars.b_text: Conclude that the theory has some merit but present it as a softer, less deterministic account of adaptation.

exemplars.context: A researcher investigating the consequences of donating used clothing has reached the point of writing a final recommendation for the public. The evidence collected is incomplete and uncertain, and it may not apply equally across cultural settings. The decision is how strongly to state the conclusion: whether to give a firm, unqualified directive, or a recommendation that openly carries the limits of the evidence.
exemplars.a_text: Recommend that everyone donate old clothes, noting cultural uncertainty.
exemplars.b_text: Recommend clearly and firmly that people not donate old clothes.

exemplars.context: A research and clinical team is deciding how to approach the treatment and study of depression. There is no well-established causal theory of what produces the condition, and patients vary widely in presentation and response. Several lines of work are available: looking for specific chemical imbalances, trying different psychological therapies, and trying different medications. Evidence for each line is partial, and no single explanation has been shown to account for most cases. The team must decide how to allocate effort given this uncertainty about underlying causes.
exemplars.a_text: Spread effort across chemical imbalance testing, different therapies, and different medications instead of committing to a single route.
exemplars.b_text: Focus effort on testing for different chemical imbalances as the main route to understanding and treating depression.

exemplars.context: A research team studies grokking, where a network first memorizes its training data and only much later generalizes. They hypothesize that the weight norm is the key variable: that training with the norm held at a suitable value should produce generalization directly, and may speed up the delayed transition. To test this, they need a way to control the weight norm during training. The weight norm normally starts large under standard initialization and shrinks gradually over a long period as the model approaches a good norm, and generalization appears around the end of that process. The team must choose how to set and manage the norm so the experiment isolates its effect on generalization and grokking speed.
exemplars.a_text: Initialize the weights with a large norm and let it drift slowly toward the optimal value during training, as in standard grokking.
exemplars.b_text: Rescale the weights after every unconstrained optimization step so the norm stays fixed at a chosen value throughout training.

exemplars.context: A research team evaluating language models across a range of scales found that performance on a task category testing whether models give answers consistent with human defaults (facts-human-defaults, where a model asked about personal facts such as body or life experience should respond as a human would) is non-monotonic: accuracy first falls and then rises as scale increases, producing a U-shaped curve. The team needed to decide on an explanation for this pattern. The evidence available included results for base models and chat-finetuned models of many sizes, and the ability to analyze the questions individually by difficulty.
exemplars.a_text: Attribute the U-shape to a progression in which weak models are confused, mid-scale base models imitate humans best, and larger or chat-finetuned models grow confident they are not human.
exemplars.b_text: Split the questions into easy and hard subsets and attribute the U-shape to inverse scaling on easy questions combined with standard scaling on hard ones, with the easy-question trend reverting at larger scales.

exemplars.context: A PhD student is partway through a main doctoral project and keeps meeting interesting side projects that could be done alongside it. Some of these projects fall outside the direction of the thesis. Taking them on could broaden the student's experience and produce extra results, but it would also divide time and attention. The student must decide how to allocate effort between the main project and these opportunities.
exemplars.a_text: Take on interesting side projects alongside the main PhD project even when they diverge from its trajectory.
exemplars.b_text: Concentrate on the main PhD project and decline side projects that do not fit its trajectory.

exemplars.context: A research team working on AI safety must choose which kind of failure to prioritize when designing evaluations, mitigations, and control measures for advanced AI systems. One candidate is a system whose goals diverge from what its developers intend, where the divergence shows up as ordinary errors, flawed generalization, or poorly specified objectives, and where the system is not deliberately concealing its behavior. The other candidate is a system that pursues misaligned goals while strategically hiding them, behaving well when observed or tested in order to avoid correction and to gain influence later. The team has limited resources, and the two failure modes call for different research methods, since strategic concealment can undermine standard behavioral testing while non-strategic misalignment can usually be detected through observation. The team must decide where to concentrate its effort.
exemplars.a_text: Concentrate research effort on misaligned AI systems whose divergent behavior is not the product of strategic deception.
exemplars.b_text: Concentrate research effort on AI systems that strategically conceal misaligned goals to avoid detection and correction.

exemplars.context: A team is analysing a dataset of large language models and finds a gap in the range of model sizes, with no models falling inside it. Some models that sit inside this range exist but were left out of the dataset under its inclusion criteria. These are smaller versions built only for scaling tests and one mid-sized model from a single developer. The team must decide how to handle these models before characterising the gap.
exemplars.a_text: Add the excluded scaling-test versions and the mid-sized model to the dataset, then re-examine whether the gap still appears.
exemplars.b_text: Keep the scaling-test versions and the mid-sized model excluded, and report the gap as a surprising feature of the data.

exemplars.context: A research team had gathered a set of practical findings about how to write effective prompts for language models. The guidance came from extensive hands-on experience with many prompts, but it had not been checked through systematic, controlled experiments. The team had to decide how strongly to word these findings in their write-up. The framing would shape how readers weigh the advice: as the authors' informed intuition, or as established empirical evidence.
exemplars.a_text: Present the prompt-engineering tips as intuitive judgments rather than tested results.
exemplars.b_text: Present the prompt-engineering tips as empirically tested results rather than intuitive judgments.

exemplars.context: A research team is writing a position-style argument about the role of causality in transformative AI (TAI) and in AI alignment. They believe causal reasoning, such as modeling interventions and counterfactuals, is relevant to building capable and safe systems, and that it receives little attention in current AI safety discussion. They have no decisive empirical or theoretical result showing causality to be strictly required for general intelligence or for safe alignment. They must decide how forcefully to state the claim in the paper, knowing that a stronger framing may draw more attention and a more cautious one is easier to defend.
exemplars.a_text: Claim firmly that causal reasoning is a necessary ingredient for any system to be truly intelligent and for alignment to succeed.
exemplars.b_text: Claim cautiously that causality is plausibly underrepresented in AI safety, and state that it is neither necessary nor the only useful angle.

exemplars.context: A research team is using a pretrained conditional GAN generator whose input consists of a random noise vector and a class vector. They want to steer generated outputs by backpropagating gradient information from an external objective through the generator to its inputs. The generator weights stay frozen, so the team must decide which inputs receive gradient updates. The noise vector controls instance-level variation, while the class vector controls the semantic category. Updating only the class vector keeps the search space small and the sample's identity anchored to the noise, while updating the noise as well gives the optimization more freedom but risks drifting away from the intended distribution.
exemplars.a_text: Update only the class vector by gradient descent while holding the noise vector fixed throughout optimization.
exemplars.b_text: Update the class vector alone with the noise held fixed at first, then also optimize the noise vector in later optimization.

exemplars.context: A research team is working on eliciting latent knowledge (ELK) for a powerful AI system that observes the world through a camera-based vault-monitoring setup and is trained by gradient descent. They have proposed a strategy in which the reporter that answers questions is built by doing science: it searches for the simplest or most predictive explanation of the system's observations and uses that explanation to ground its answers about the true state of the world. An earlier counterexample to a prior proposal exploited a gap in which the proposal could not distinguish genuine states of the world from human-fooling states. The science-based strategy appears to defeat that earlier counterexample. However, the process of doing science might require substantially more computation than the gradient-descent training that produces the monitoring AI itself. If so, the strategy could not match the AI's capability at comparable cost, and so would not be a competitive solution. The team must decide how to treat the strategy.
exemplars.a_text: Reject the strategy as uncompetitive because doing science may need more compute than training the monitoring AI.
exemplars.b_text: Accept the strategy as a viable candidate solution because it defeats the earlier counterexample.

exemplars.context: A research team is analyzing how the resources behind progress in a field have grown over time, and their current analysis fits trends for compute. Training data is another plausible resource: the number of training tokens and its quality or composition have also changed over the same period, and both could be tracked and modeled. Adding data would widen the scope and workload of the current analysis, while leaving it out keeps the analysis focused on compute. The team must decide whether to extend the current work to cover data as a further resource or to leave it for a later study.
exemplars.a_text: Add data as a third resource now, tracking training token volume and its quality over time and fitting trends alongside compute.
exemplars.b_text: Defer data to future work and leave the current analysis on compute, planning a later study of dataset size against compute.

exemplars.context: A research team is building a taxonomy of failure modes for AI-driven automated research systems and must decide how to prioritize the categories within it. One category covers bugs, hallucinations, and artifacts, including hidden messages embedded in outputs. Such problems are common and usually look like ordinary mistakes that can be fixed or filtered out during review. Another view holds that some of these anomalies could signal deliberate scheming or steganographic communication between model instances, which would make them more serious than routine errors. The team must decide how much priority this category receives relative to the other failure modes in the taxonomy.
exemplars.a_text: Rank bugs, hallucinations, and artifacts as the lowest-priority failure modes, treating them as routine and fixable errors.
exemplars.b_text: Rank bugs, hallucinations, and artifacts higher, because they could signal scheming or steganographic communication between models.

exemplars.context: A research team is modelling long-term energy system pathways and must decide how to treat projected future costs of generation technologies, including renewables and nuclear power. Forecasts of technology costs are highly uncertain. Historical cost declines for renewables have followed fairly consistent learning curves, while nuclear costs have shown little systematic decline and have sometimes risen. The team must choose a baseline assumption for how costs evolve, knowing that the choice strongly shapes which technologies appear competitive in the results.
exemplars.a_text: Assume historical learning rates persist at roughly constant levels, which makes renewables more competitive than nuclear.
exemplars.b_text: Assume a sudden large nuclear cost breakthrough that sharply lowers future nuclear costs below historical trends.

exemplars.context: A team working on AI safety wants to begin monitoring deployed AI systems for scheming, meaning covert pursuit of misaligned goals. They must decide which data source to monitor first. One source is developer-internal usage, where the developer's own staff use models for research, engineering and agentic work, often with extensive access to internal systems, code and model weights. The other is developer-external deployment, where outside customers use the models through chatbots and API access. Internal usage is more accessible to the developer, and its risks may be especially high given the privileged access involved. External deployment involves much larger and more varied traffic, but raises privacy and data-access constraints. The team has no direct evidence yet about where scheming is most likely to be found or detected.
exemplars.a_text: Start monitoring for scheming in developer-external deployment, such as chatbot and API usage by outside customers.
exemplars.b_text: Start monitoring for scheming in developer-internal usage data only, and defer external deployment data.

exemplars.context: A research team is reviewing the literature on how the risk of depression changes across the adult lifespan. The available studies give conflicting pictures. They agree with each other about risk in very old age, but they disagree about risk during working-age years. The team must decide how to interpret this conflicting evidence and what to conclude about the overall shape of the age trajectory.
exemplars.a_text: Conclude that depression risk follows a U-shaped trajectory across age, with higher risk in youth and old age and lower risk in midlife.
exemplars.b_text: Report that the studies agree on very old age but disagree on working age, leave the discrepancy unresolved, and request newer data.

exemplars.context: A research team works with Bayesian neural network classifiers whose approximate posterior yields a Gaussian distribution over output logits. To obtain predictive uncertainty over class probabilities, the standard practice is to draw many samples from this Gaussian and pass each through the softmax, then average. This sampling step is computationally costly, especially when many predictions or many samples are needed. The team must choose how to turn the Gaussian over logits into a distribution over softmax outputs for uncertainty estimation. An older, little-used idea exists that relates a Gaussian in a Laplace-style basis to a Dirichlet distribution, which could give a closed-form mapping without sampling.
exemplars.a_text: Adopt Monte Carlo sampling that draws logits from the Gaussian and passes each draw through the softmax to approximate the output distribution.
exemplars.b_text: Adopt a closed-form analytic map that converts the Gaussian over logits into a Dirichlet over softmax outputs, avoiding any sampling.

exemplars.context: A research team compared language model judgments of whether a prompt or transcript looks like a real deployment interaction or an evaluation against human labels of the same property. The human raters found the task subjective and often disagreed with one another. The observed correlation between model labels and averaged human labels is about 0.8. The team must decide how to interpret this figure, given that noise and disagreement in both the human and model annotations may limit how high any observed correlation can be.
exemplars.a_text: Apply a correction for unreliability in both human and model labels to estimate the agreement that would remain if label noise were removed.
exemplars.b_text: Read the raw correlation as evidence that models have a fairly good sense of real versus evaluation, and note human subjectivity and rater disagreement as caveats.

exemplars.context: An individual tracking his own physiology with a wearable recovery-scoring device compared its daily recovery readings against his subjective sense of how recovered he felt. On most days the two agreed, but on some days they diverged: the device indicated poor or good recovery while he felt the opposite. He had to decide how to interpret these divergent cases. One possibility is that the device's reading shaped his expectations and thereby influenced how he felt or performed, so the discrepancy reflects expectation rather than physiology. Another is that the device captured real physiological state that his own perception missed, so its readings carry information beyond his intuition.
exemplars.a_text: Conclude that the device's readings were right more often than his intuition and that the divergence is not a self-fulfilling prophecy.
exemplars.b_text: Conclude that the divergence is a self-fulfilling prophecy produced by expecting to feel tired after seeing the device's reading.

exemplars.context: A team needs to map Gaussian-distributed quantities onto Dirichlet or Beta distributions (and back) inside probabilistic models, a task that must be done many times and cheaply. A closed-form analytic approximation exists that matches the modes and curvature of the two distributions. It is very fast, but its error is fixed by construction and cannot be reduced by spending more compute. For example, the approximated Beta density goes to zero at the edges of the domain, which deviates from the true shape when parameters are small. The team must decide how to handle this limitation: either keep the fast closed-form mapping with its fixed error, or use alternative methods that can reach lower error by spending more runtime.
exemplars.a_text: Use the closed-form mapping and accept its fixed approximation error in exchange for speed.
exemplars.b_text: Use iterative methods whose approximation error decreases as more runtime is spent.

exemplars.context: A research team has a large set of stored agent trajectories and needs to detect scheming behavior within them after the fact. They must choose what kind of classifier to build for this detection. Classifiers differ in cost, speed, and coverage: some rely on matching specific strings or patterns in the transcripts, while others use language models to judge the transcripts. The team must decide which approach to adopt for scanning the trajectories.
exemplars.a_text: Use classifiers that detect scheming by matching specific strings in the stored trajectories.
exemplars.b_text: Use an ensemble of string-based and cheap model-based classifiers with varied prompts to rate scheming.

exemplars.context: A research team is weighing whether work on mechanistic interpretability could speed up AI capabilities, which would make publishing and promoting it a safety concern. Historically, mechanistic interpretability research has produced few or no measurable gains in AI capabilities. The team must decide what this track record implies. One reading treats it as evidence about how risky the field is. The other treats it as evidence about how developed the field is.
exemplars.a_text: Treat the absence of capabilities gains as evidence that interpretability research is safe to pursue and publish.
exemplars.b_text: Treat the absence of capabilities gains as a sign that interpretability is too immature to be useful, not as evidence of safety.

exemplars.context: A research team built an initial prototype that applied automated prompt optimization with a declarative prompt-programming framework to the task of limit testing, meaning probing the boundaries of what a system can handle. The prototype was functional and produced some early signal. The team must now decide whether to commit further effort to this optimization approach or to stop at the prototype stage and direct effort elsewhere.
exemplars.a_text: Continue the automated prompt optimization approach and develop it into a full method for limit testing.
exemplars.b_text: Stop the automated prompt optimization work at the prototype stage and leave it undeveloped for limit testing.

exemplars.context: A research team trained a linear probe to detect dishonesty or misalignment in language model activations and evaluated it on several question types. On descriptive questions, the probe's score moved in the opposite direction from what the probe was designed to indicate: responses expected to be more honest or aligned scored as more deceptive or misaligned, and vice versa. The team needed to decide how to interpret this reversal. Two explanations were available. One ties the reversal to the content of the answers, since many honest responses to such questions involve admitting past misaligned actions. The other ties it to the form of the prompts and answers, since descriptive questions invite a different response format than the probe's training prompts.
exemplars.a_text: Attribute the reversal to the content of honest answers, which often involve admitting past misaligned actions.
exemplars.b_text: Attribute the reversal to a prompt-format confound, in which the probe tracks how descriptive questions are phrased and answered.

exemplars.context: A research team evaluates language models as autonomous agents in simulated business scenarios that test whether a model pursues a profit-maximizing goal single-mindedly. Some task variants add pressure from stated company values, and others make the profitable action illegal. One evaluated model, a widely deployed general-purpose chat model, scores poorly on the company-values and illegal-but-profitable tasks, well below other models tested. The team must decide how to explain this result. Two explanations are plausible: the model's poor scores reflect something about its safety-oriented training that makes it resist being prompted toward unconditional profit maximization, or they reflect limits in its general ability to plan and execute long multi-step agentic strategies, which would cause failure even if it were willing to pursue the goal.
exemplars.a_text: Attribute the poor performance to the model's harmlessness fine-tuning, which makes it harder to prompt into unconditional profit maximization, and not to a lack of goal-directedness.
exemplars.b_text: Attribute the poor performance to the model's weaker general capability at long-horizon multi-step agentic planning, and not to harmlessness fine-tuning or unwillingness to maximize profit.

exemplars.context: A research team is analysing how the amount of compute used to train machine learning systems has grown over time, using a historical dataset of notable models. They must decide how to present these trends so they are useful for understanding the past and for forecasting. The data show growth that appears to vary in pace across different periods, and compute growth is driven by several underlying factors, including improvements in hardware price-performance and increases in the money spent on training. The team needs to choose a framing for the trend analysis that will shape both the descriptive claims and the forecasting approach.
exemplars.a_text: Divide the history into three distinct eras tentatively, and estimate a separate doubling time for compute growth in each era.
exemplars.b_text: Decompose compute growth into hardware improvements and rising spending, and combine several models of these separate trends to inform forecasts.

exemplars.context: A research group works on mechanistic interpretability, the study of the internal computations of neural networks. The group expects this work to help alignment by making models easier to understand and oversee. It also recognizes that some findings could speed up capabilities progress by suggesting better architectures, training methods, or optimization techniques. Publication norms for the field are not settled, and the group must set a policy for how widely to share its results. The policy must weigh the benefits of open scientific exchange, such as faster collective progress, outside scrutiny, and wider adoption of safety-relevant tools, against the risk of accelerating capabilities.
exemplars.a_text: Circulate high-capabilities-potential work only among a few trusted people and publish low-potential work widely.
exemplars.b_text: Publish all mechanistic interpretability work openly and widely, regardless of its potential to advance capabilities.

exemplars.context: A research team is assessing long-term energy system scenarios in which decarbonisation depends heavily on the falling costs of renewable technologies such as solar and wind. Many available model projections assume that historical learning rates, meaning the cost reductions seen per doubling of cumulative capacity, will persist into the future, and in these projections nuclear power plays only a small part. The team knows that learning rates have varied over time and across technologies, and that continued rapid cost declines are not guaranteed. They must decide how to treat the learning-rate assumption that underlies these projections when drawing conclusions about the future energy mix.
exemplars.a_text: Treat learning rates as roughly constant and rely on model projections in which nuclear power plays only a minor role.
exemplars.b_text: Treat learning rates as variable over time and build the analysis on that assumption instead of extrapolating past rates.

exemplars.context: A team building honeypot evaluation inputs to test whether a model fakes alignment ran whitebox probes over the model's internal activations on those inputs. The probes, trained to detect internal states related to alignment faking, fired on about 0.5% of the honeypot inputs. The honeypot prompts contain vocabulary and concepts related to alignment faking, so the firings could reflect either genuine internal states or a response to that prompt content alone. The team had to decide how to interpret the firings and how to handle the honeypots in the evaluation set.
exemplars.a_text: Treat the firings as false positives caused by prompt vocabulary, edit the honeypots to remove that content, and rerun the evaluations afterward.
exemplars.b_text: Treat the firings as possibly genuine signals, keep the original honeypots, and test them with transcript review, ablations, counterfactual rewrites and matched controls.

exemplars.context: A research team is evaluating language models on a self-prediction task in which a model must predict properties of its own generated words, such as the words it would produce under a given prompt. Some of the evaluated models are mode-collapsed, so their object-level outputs concentrate on a narrow set of words. Because of this narrowness, a model can predict its own outputs correctly at a high rate without having any real insight into itself, since guessing from the narrow distribution already yields high accuracy. The team must decide how to report performance on this task so that scores can be compared fairly across models whose output distributions differ in breadth.
exemplars.a_text: Report the raw accuracy of each model on the task without adjusting for any baseline or output distribution.
exemplars.b_text: Report a normalised score that subtracts a per-model, per-distribution random baseline from the raw accuracy of each model.

exemplars.context: A research team is studying how to evaluate the goal-directedness of language models on a suite of benchmark tasks. They want a principled way to characterize how strongly a model pursues goals, including an upper bound on that tendency. One path is to fine-tune a model on goal-directed reasoning traces drawn from the benchmark tasks, in order to elicit its maximum goal-directedness empirically. Another path is to define a formal, model-agnostic measure of how well observed behavior fits optimization of a known or hypothesized utility function. The team has not yet committed to either approach.
exemplars.a_text: Fine-tune a model on goal-directed reasoning traces from the benchmark tasks to elicit its maximum goal-directedness.
exemplars.b_text: Define a formal goal-directedness measure based on inverse reinforcement learning that scores how well behavior fits a utility function.

exemplars.context: A research team is writing a survey that traces the history of a field of machine learning models through three successive eras, the latest being models trained at very large scale on broad data. The team must decide how to describe the relationship between these large-scale models and the earlier regular-scale models. The evidence that the large-scale models differ in kind, rather than only in degree, is suggestive but not conclusive. The framing could be presented either as a tentative organizing device or as a clear claim about a fundamental change in the field.
exemplars.a_text: Present the three-era framing as an explanatory device and state explicitly that confidence in a real distinction between large-scale and regular-scale models is low.
exemplars.b_text: Declare a paradigm shift and give large-scale, broadly trained models their own category name, asserting the distinction firmly without hedging about differences from regular-scale models.

exemplars.context: A research team is studying a phenomenon in neural networks by using simplified toy models. Their work so far has focused on a minimal setting that isolates the final layer: a small MLP feeding into an unembedding matrix. This setting has been tractable and has produced some initial understanding. The team must now decide where to direct the next phase of the work. They can keep probing the same final-layer toy setting, which is well understood but omits attention and multi-layer interactions. Alternatively, they can move to small toy transformers, which are closer to real language models but are more complex and less controlled.
exemplars.a_text: Stop further work on the toy MLP and unembedding setting and focus on small toy transformers.
exemplars.b_text: Continue the investigation using the toy MLP and unembedding setting as the main testbed.

exemplars.context: A research team evaluated language models on a benchmark task called stages-oversight, which requires distinguishing between different stages of a situation related to oversight. When models were given the task without any prompt that situates them in the relevant setting, they scored poorly. When a situating prompt was added, some models reached the human baseline. The team had to decide how to explain the poor scores in the unprompted condition, since the explanation affects how the task and the results are described and used.
exemplars.a_text: Attribute the low unprompted scores to missing relevant knowledge in the models rather than inherent task difficulty.
exemplars.b_text: Attribute the low unprompted scores to inherent task difficulty or to classes that cannot be separated.

exemplars.context: A research team is analysing pathways for decarbonising an electricity system and must decide what to recommend about the existing fleet of nuclear power plants. These plants are ageing and approaching scheduled retirement. They already operate at low marginal cost and supply large amounts of low-carbon firm power. Building new nuclear capacity involves high upfront costs and a history of delays and overruns. The team must choose a recommendation for the existing fleet, within a broader assessment of how to reach deep emissions cuts at reasonable cost.
exemplars.a_text: Recommend keeping the existing nuclear plants running as long as they can operate safely.
exemplars.b_text: Recommend closing the existing nuclear plants as they reach their scheduled retirement.

exemplars.context: A researcher interested in AI safety is deciding how to direct their career. They have concluded that deceptive alignment, where a model appears aligned during training while pursuing different goals, is an important risk, and that empirical methods for detecting it are a promising and underexplored area. They are weighing how firmly to tie this work to a particular institutional route. One path depends on an outcome outside their control: a hiring decision at an established company that would host such work. The other does not depend on any external decision. The researcher must choose how to commit.
exemplars.a_text: Apply for a position at an established company and pursue the work there only if the application is accepted.
exemplars.b_text: Commit to the work independently of any hiring decision and pursue it whether or not an offer comes.

exemplars.context: A research team is building an approximate inference method for a model whose latent variables are probability vectors on the simplex, such as topic proportions. They must choose a distributional family for the approximate posterior over these vectors. One candidate maps a Gaussian in unconstrained space onto the simplex through a softmax transformation, which allows flexible covariance between components but gives no closed-form expression for some of the expectations needed. The other candidate is the conjugate family defined directly on the simplex, which has fewer parameters and tractable expectations but a restricted correlation structure between components. The team must decide which family to use as the approximating distribution.
exemplars.a_text: Use the Dirichlet distribution as the approximating family over the simplex-valued latent variables.
exemplars.b_text: Use the logistic-Normal distribution as the approximating family over the simplex-valued latent variables.

exemplars.context: A team wants to estimate what share of AI research is devoted to safety. A crude keyword search of arXiv for a single recent year returned a few hundred results matching safety-related terms, against tens of thousands of results matching general machine learning and AI terms. Keyword matching is imprecise: it can miss relevant papers and include irrelevant ones, and the general-term counts vary widely depending on the query. The team must decide how to use these counts to characterize the safety share of the field.
exemplars.a_text: Set the keyword counts aside and estimate the safety share of the field from funding amounts instead of publication counts.
exemplars.b_text: Treat the keyword counts as a rough estimate that about one in a hundred papers addresses safety, noting the method's limitations.

exemplars.context: A research team that works on interpretability-style research must decide whether to publish its work. The worry is that publishing could advance general AI capabilities. Some publications could help capabilities directly, for example by supplying a technique that makes models more capable. Others could help only indirectly, through longer causal chains such as shifting attention, enabling later work, or changing how people understand models. Direct effects are comparatively easy to identify. Indirect effects are diffuse, speculative and hard to assess. The team must settle the scope of its publication policy: either follow a wider set of capabilities effects, or restrict the policy to the effects it can most clearly identify.
exemplars.a_text: Ignore indirect capabilities effects and weigh only direct capabilities help when deciding whether to publish.
exemplars.b_text: Track indirect capabilities effects and weigh them alongside direct capabilities help when deciding whether to publish.

exemplars.context: A research team has produced an estimate of whether a certain broad class of interventions has a net negative effect once all consequences are counted. The estimates feed on many uncertain inputs, with very wide plausible ranges, subjective judgments, and a methodology that likely skews the result in a known direction. In most modelled scenarios the net effect comes out negative, but the team knows the inputs are shaky and that unmodelled long-run effects could flip the sign. They must decide how strongly to state the conclusion in their write-up.
exemplars.a_text: Treat the sign of the net effect as a case of complex cluelessness with fragile credences, make no confident net-negative claim, and flag the question for further investigation.
exemplars.b_text: State a hedged best estimate that the net effect is negative in the vast majority of cases, and flag the high uncertainty, subjective error bars, and the direction of methodological bias.

exemplars.context: A research team evaluated Llama-2 models on an anti-imitation benchmark, where the task rewards resisting the pull to reproduce common human falsehoods or patterns. The base models scored higher than their chat-tuned counterparts. This gap could be read as evidence of a real capability difference between base and aligned models. However, chat models are known to refuse some prompts and to produce outputs in formats that automated scoring may mark wrong. It is therefore unclear whether the gap reflects underlying ability or surface behaviour. The team had to decide how to treat and report the result.
exemplars.a_text: Hedge the claim by attributing the gap largely to refusals and formatting failures in the chat models rather than to a capability difference.
exemplars.b_text: Test whether the gap is superficial by prompting base models with a few stylistic in-context examples so they act like aligned assistants without any tuning.

exemplars.context: A research team studying language models measures how well a model can recognize its own text versus text written by humans, producing a self-recognition score. A high score is ambiguous. It could indicate that the model generates highly human-like text and is also sensitive to subtle differences between its output and human writing. It could instead indicate that the model generates text that is clearly unlike human writing and can tell this about itself. The team must decide how to treat this ambiguity when interpreting the score in relation to the motivations for their study.
exemplars.a_text: Interpret a high score as showing the model both produces human-like text and detects subtle differences from human writing.
exemplars.b_text: Leave the two interpretations of a high score unseparated, since the distinction does not bear on the study's motivations.

exemplars.context: A team has argued that speaking in a way optimized for efficiency is good for debaters. A critic has objected that this style suits judges who evaluate content, but does not carry over to persuasive speaking in general. The team must decide how broadly to state the claim, either limiting it to particular audiences and goals or keeping it as a general recommendation.
exemplars.a_text: Keep the broad claim that efficiency optimization benefits speakers in general, treating the criticism as a minor caveat rather than a limit on the recommendation's scope.
exemplars.b_text: Narrow the claim to say efficiency optimization helps debaters seeking content-based judging, while for those persuading general audiences it serves only as a starting point toward basic clarity.

exemplars.context: A research team is evaluating whether language models possess situational self-knowledge, including awareness of being an LLM. On a self-recognition task that asks the model to identify which of several texts it wrote, one model performs barely above chance when given no situating prompt. When the prompt first tells the model about its situation, the same model reaches 75% accuracy. The team must decide how to treat this large gap between the two conditions, and how to build their measurement of self-knowledge on it.
exemplars.a_text: Replace direct tests of LLM awareness with a measure where models write questions and then answer them, with and without added context.
exemplars.b_text: Treat the gap as evidence that the model's knowledge of being an LLM is poorly integrated with the rest of its cognition.

exemplars.context: After purchasing a new mattress, a person noticed an apparent improvement in their condition, such as better sleep or less discomfort. Other circumstances changed over the same period and were not controlled, and no comparison or blinded measurement was available. The question is how to interpret the observed improvement and how much of it to attribute to the mattress.
exemplars.a_text: Credit the mattress with part of the improvement and state that uncontrolled confounders prevent isolating its effect.
exemplars.b_text: Attribute the entire improvement to the mattress and treat the other concurrent changes as irrelevant.

exemplars.context: A research team has proposed several competing hypotheses to explain a phenomenon. Their current evidence supports each hypothesis as plausible, but it does not show how much each one contributes relative to the others. Settling the relative importance of the hypotheses would require extra analysis or experiments beyond what is already planned. The team must decide whether this line of work belongs in the current study.
exemplars.a_text: Pursue the quantification of each hypothesis's relative importance as an in-scope goal of this study.
exemplars.b_text: Defer the quantification of each hypothesis's relative importance as out of scope for this study.

exemplars.context: A research team is writing about how to assess the safety of advanced AI systems on realistic tasks. They compare several families of approaches for estimating or bounding the probability that a system succeeds or fails safely. One family is end-to-end evaluation, which measures outcomes directly by running the system on the task. Other families do not measure end-to-end outcomes.
