These include formal verification against a specified world model and safety specification, component-wise analysis, and interpretability-based arguments. The team has concluded that these non-end-to-end approaches have significant limitations for realistic tasks, such as gaps between the model and the real world and difficulty composing component-level results. They must decide how forcefully to present this conclusion in the paper, and which position to put forward regarding the role of the non-end-to-end approaches in critical decisions.
exemplars.a_text: State that no method other than end-to-end evaluation can reliably estimate or bound success probability on realistic tasks, and that such methods should not inform critical decisions.
exemplars.b_text: Advocate formally specifying a world model and safety specification, then using a verifier to produce auditable proof certificates or quantitative bounds in place of end-to-end empirical estimation.

exemplars.context: A team is writing a post about causality in machine learning systems. There is no settled technical understanding of what causality means in this setting, and different communities use the term in different ways. The team must fix a working definition of causality to use throughout the post, since the definition determines which systems and capabilities count as causal and which do not.
exemplars.a_text: Adopt a broad working definition in which causality can be learned from data and need not be explicitly represented, so it may reside in learned model parameters.
exemplars.b_text: Adopt a narrow working definition in which causality counts only when humans explicitly specify the causal structure and build it into the model.

exemplars.context: A research team studying the global trade in a commodity abbreviated SHC examined import data and found that countries in Asia, rather than countries in Africa, are the largest importers. Public and policy discussion had given heavy emphasis to African imports as a major driver of the trade. The team had to decide how to interpret the mismatch between the data and the prevailing narrative: whether it indicates that the narrative has long overstated the role of African imports, or whether it reflects a recent, sharp shift in the pattern of imports that the narrative has not caught up with.
exemplars.a_text: Conclude that the debate overstates the importance of African imports and reject the idea that the import picture changed recently.
exemplars.b_text: Conclude that the import picture has changed drastically in recent years and that the debate reflects an outdated pattern.

exemplars.context: A review team is assessing the ethics and risks of genetic modification across living organisms. Having already weighed the benefits, harms and uncertainties for genetically modified plants, the team now turns to animals. The animal case involves additional considerations, including animal welfare, sentience, ecological effects of release, and less established evidence of benefit relative to the plant case. The team must decide how firmly to state its overall conclusion on genetically modifying animals, given that the balance of considerations is harder to judge and more uncertain here than for plants.
exemplars.a_text: Conclude in favor of genetically modifying animals while stating that the weighing is harder and less certain than for plants.
exemplars.b_text: Conclude against genetically modifying animals, stating that the risks and welfare concerns outweigh the benefits.

exemplars.context: A research team is comparing the performance of automated systems on full end-to-end task runs against earlier estimates derived from intermediate milestones. The milestone estimates rest on specific assumptions about how each stage proceeds, such as each stage receiving correct inputs from the previous one. The team must decide how to score the end-to-end runs for this comparison. One scoring approach strictly enforces the milestone assumptions, so a run is credited only if it follows the idealized path. Another approach looks only at whether the final answer is correct, which is closer to how such systems would be used in practice but does not enforce those assumptions. The choice affects how directly the end-to-end results can be matched to the milestone estimates and how well they reflect realistic use.
exemplars.a_text: Score every end-to-end run twice, using idealized grading that enforces the milestone assumptions and outcome-based grading that checks only the final answer.
exemplars.b_text: Score every end-to-end run using only idealized grading, which enforces the milestone assumptions and credits runs that follow the idealized path.

exemplars.context: A research team analysed a dataset of GPU and AI accelerator prices and performance spanning many years, aiming to quantify how quickly price-performance improves. They measured a doubling time for price-performance as a function of calendar time. Commonly cited benchmarks for comparison are Moore's law, which implies a doubling roughly every two years for transistor density, and Huang's law, which claims much faster GPU performance gains. Earlier published estimates of GPU price-performance improvement were also available and suggested slower progress. The team had to decide how to frame and interpret their measured improvement rate: either by directly comparing the fitted calendar-time doubling rate against these reference laws and prior estimates, or by adopting a different explanatory model that ties cost reduction to cumulative production rather than to elapsed time.
exemplars.a_text: Explain the rapid price-performance gains with a learning curve in which cost falls as cumulative production grows, rather than a calendar-time doubling rate.
exemplars.b_text: Report the fitted calendar-time doubling rate and state that it is slightly slower than Moore's law, much slower than Huang's law, and considerably faster than prior estimates.

exemplars.context: A research team studies memorization of individual training samples in a trained neural model. They computed cosine similarity between embeddings as a candidate signal for whether a sample has been memorized, and examined the results across samples. The similarity values did not separate samples in an obviously clean way, so the team had to decide how to interpret these results and whether to keep relying on embedding similarity as the basis for detecting memorization or to move to a different kind of measure. An alternative available to them was a per-sample score based on the local geometry of the loss around each training example, tracked over the course of training.
exemplars.a_text: Conclude that plain cosine similarity between embeddings is not a reliable detector of memorization and stop using it as one.
exemplars.b_text: Score each training sample's memorization by the loss curvature around it, averaged over training epochs, instead of by embedding similarity.

exemplars.context: A research team evaluated a milestone-based method for estimating how many trainees reach a competency benchmark across a set of subcompetencies. The method assumes milestones form a fixed, ordered sequence that trainees pass through in turn. When the team compared the method's estimates with outcome-based grading, in which each trainee is graded directly on whether the benchmark was achieved, the milestone method produced systematically lower estimates of achievement. The benchmark was a single uniform target rating applied to every subcompetency, and many graduating trainees did not reach it. The team had to decide how to interpret the underestimation.
exemplars.a_text: Attribute the shortfall to the demanding uniform benchmark that many graduating trainees did not meet, not to flawed assumptions in the milestone method.
exemplars.b_text: Attribute the shortfall to the milestone method's assumption of a fixed, ordered sequence failing in practice, which causes systematic underestimation.

exemplars.context: A research team is working on Inverse Classification, the task of generating or adjusting inputs so that a trained classifier assigns them to a desired class. They have already tried an LSTM-based approach to the problem and now must decide which generative model family to pursue next as the core of their method. The choice determines the architecture used to produce candidate inputs for the target class, and the team can commit to only one direction for the next stage of work.
exemplars.a_text: Use LSTMs as the generative model for Inverse Classification.
exemplars.b_text: Use conditional GANs as the generative model for Inverse Classification.

exemplars.context: A team is assessing whether an expert best-of-N method gives results usable for safety-relevant decisions. In this method, a human expert picks the best of N model attempts at a task, and the amount of selection needed is expressed as a number of bits. The team wants to use these bit counts to estimate how likely a model is to solve a task. The estimate depends on an assumed prior over solve rates, and the bit counts are not by themselves probabilities. The team must decide how to treat the method as an estimator of task solve rate.
exemplars.a_text: Reject expert best-of-N as an estimator of task solve rate, because its bit counts do not map to calibrated probabilities.
exemplars.b_text: Keep expert best-of-N as an estimator of task solve rate, and convert its bit counts into calibrated probabilities by using a different prior.

exemplars.context: A research team has been building model organisms to study whether AI systems that reason in a consequentialist way, pursuing outcomes over following rules, develop scheming behaviour such as hiding goals or acting deceptively to reach them. They have produced early demonstrations and have a sense of how tractable and informative the setup is. They must now decide how to allocate their effort going forward. Continuing would keep the team's time and resources committed to this line of work. Stepping back would free those resources for other priorities, and the work could still be taken up by outside groups if the team shared what it has built and learned.
exemplars.a_text: Pause the project and invite outside researchers to take the work forward.
exemplars.b_text: Keep the project going and continue the team's own work on it.

exemplars.context: A research team is analysing a time series that shows a clear acceleration in growth after 2018. The post-2018 data points fall into two groups, one below and one above a visible gap. The acceleration can be described either by a single exponential trend across all post-2018 points or by two separate trends, one for the points below the gap and one for those above it. The two-trend description adds free parameters and a split chosen after seeing the data, so it risks overfitting. The single-trend description is simpler but may fit the two groups poorly. The team must decide how to interpret the post-2018 acceleration.
exemplars.a_text: Fit one exponential trend to all post-2018 data and treat the acceleration as a single continuous process without any split.
exemplars.b_text: Split the post-2018 data into separate below-gap and above-gap trends and accept the overfitting risk that the split carries.

exemplars.context: A group asked to take a public position on tobacco control must decide how to respond to the idea of prohibiting cigarettes altogether. Smoking is a leading cause of preventable disease and death. Prohibition would remove the main product at its source, but it raises concerns about enforcement, illicit markets, and public acceptance. Other measures are also available: progressively higher tobacco taxes, public education campaigns, and restrictions on smoking in public places. The group must choose which stance to back.
exemplars.a_text: Decline an outright ban and support gradually increasing tobacco taxes alongside campaigns and smoke-free policies.
exemplars.b_text: Endorse an outright ban on cigarette sales instead of relying on incremental tax, campaign and smoke-free measures.

exemplars.context: A climate strategy team must decide what should anchor its approach to reducing emissions. One framing treats large corporations as the central adversary, with campaigns, pressure and confrontation aimed at major emitters as the main lever. The alternative framing moves away from singling out corporations and relies on market-based mechanisms, such as emissions caps with tradable permits, that change incentives across the whole economy. The team knows that emissions come from many sources, that corporate opposition has slowed past policy efforts, and that broad incentive mechanisms have a mixed record of political feasibility and effectiveness. It must choose which framing will serve as the core of its strategy.
exemplars.a_text: Replace the corporation-focused framing with cap-and-trade style incentives as the strategy's core approach.
exemplars.b_text: Keep the fight against large corporations as the central organizing principle of the climate strategy.

exemplars.context: A team working on the evaluation (evals) of AI systems wants to grow the field by attracting more researchers and building a stronger community. A neighbouring research area, mechanistic interpretability, grew quickly after a deliberate community-building effort, and that effort's methods are documented as a playbook. The team must decide whether to model its field-building strategy on that playbook or to pursue a different approach.
exemplars.a_text: Pursue an alternative field-building approach for evals that departs from the interpretability community-building playbook.
exemplars.b_text: Adopt the community-building playbook used for mechanistic interpretability and apply it to growing the evals field.

exemplars.context: A research team is benchmarking a set of language models and wants to include chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting in the evaluation. CoT evaluations cost much more than standard evaluations because each response is longer, and it is hard to design a single CoT prompt format that works consistently across every model in the set. The team has already settled on running the standard, non-CoT evaluation on every model. They must now decide how widely to apply CoT evaluation, given limited compute and the difficulty of prompting uniformly.
exemplars.a_text: Run CoT evaluation on every model in the set despite the added cost and prompting difficulty.
exemplars.b_text: Run CoT evaluation on only a small subset of two models and leave comprehensive CoT evaluation to future work.

exemplars.context: A research team working on the relationship between causal and correlational claims faced a conceptual worry: causality might be nothing more than a particular shade or special case of correlation, in which case the distinction between causal and correlational relationships would be empty and the framework built on it would lose its meaning. No empirical result bears on the question; it is a matter of how to interpret the foundations of the framework. The team had to decide how to treat this possibility, either by adopting a stance that settles whether causality exists as a distinct notion, or by accepting the reductive view that causality reduces to correlation together with chance.
exemplars.a_text: Treat causality as a genuinely distinct notion by arguing from parsimony that it is more likely to exist than not.
exemplars.b_text: Treat causality as a non-distinct notion by defining it as correlation combined with chance coincidence.

exemplars.context: A research team is building a evaluation subset from a large benchmark suite by drawing a sample of 100 questions from a pool of 1042 filtered questions. The suite contains many constructed-language translation tasks, and these question types occur so frequently that they would make up a large share of any random sample. The team must decide how to draw the sample given this imbalance in question-type frequency.
exemplars.a_text: Down-weight frequently occurring question types, then sample questions from the filtered pool.
exemplars.b_text: Sample questions uniformly from the pool and apply no reweighting to frequent question types.

exemplars.context: A research team is assessing the economic impact of donating second-hand clothing to lower-income regions where local textile and garment industries have declined. Public debate often links donated clothing directly to that decline, but the evidence is mixed and several factors operate at once. The team must decide how to frame the economic analysis and which kind of evidence to rely on in order to judge how much donated clothing actually affects local markets, workers and consumers.
exemplars.a_text: Organize the analysis around three questions on the causes of textile decline, the effects on jobs, and the benefits to consumers, to gauge how donated clothing affects local markets.
exemplars.b_text: Use trade-flow statistics, such as import values and the donor country's share of total used-clothing exports to the region, to gauge how much donated clothing affects local markets.

exemplars.context: A team wants to build probes that detect scheming in AI models, but no ground-truth labeled data exists showing when a model is actually scheming. They need a way to construct a 'scheming' representation in activation space without such labels. They have access to model activations and can generate or collect text datasets, including texts describing scheming entities and texts describing honest entities. The choice of construction method determines what direction the probes will treat as the scheming signal.
exemplars.a_text: Build the scheming feature vector from the difference in average activations between descriptions of scheming entities and descriptions of honest entities.
exemplars.b_text: Build the scheming feature vector from a classifier trained on activations from synthetic transcripts labeled as scheming or non-scheming model behavior.

exemplars.context: A research team is analysing whether the supply of training data will constrain the future scaling of multimodal models. They have rough estimates of the total amount of image and video data available, but the quantity of that data that is of high quality for training is unclear and depends on contested quality criteria. They must decide how far the analysis of image data goes: whether to go beyond total volume and also quantify the high-quality portion, or to restrict the analysis to aggregate totals.
exemplars.a_text: Restrict the analysis to total image data volume and skip any estimate of the high-quality stock.
exemplars.b_text: Estimate the size of the high-quality image data stock in addition to the total volume.

exemplars.context: A research team is building synthetic datasets for studying how language model responses differ between two conditions. They generated topical prompts derived from a set of hand-written examples (HWEs) and used them during an earlier stage to close the divergence between the responses produced under the two conditions. The team must now decide what role these topical prompts play in the final data generation step. The prompts are known to help align response behaviour, but they are also derived from the hand-written examples rather than being independent of them, so their presence in the final datasets could shape the datasets' composition and distribution.
exemplars.a_text: Remove the topical prompts from final generation and use them only to close the response divergence.
exemplars.b_text: Keep the topical prompts derived from the hand-written examples in the final datasets alongside the other prompts.

exemplars.context: A research team is training linear probes on a language model's internal activations to detect a target concept. Several standard ways of fitting the probe direction are available: logistic regression, difference of class means, linear discriminant analysis, and a principal-component-based approach on activation differences. The team has compared these candidates and must now choose a single method to use as the default probe-fitting approach for the main experiments.
exemplars.a_text: Use difference of class means as the default probe-fitting method for the main experiments.
exemplars.b_text: Use logistic regression as the default probe-fitting method for the main experiments.

exemplars.context: A research team evaluated a language model with in-context examples, where the order of elements within the demonstration shots differed from the order used in the final test prompt. Performance was worse in this mismatched condition. In addition, prompts with several shots scored lower than prompts with a single shot. The team had to decide how to explain this drop and the k-shot versus one-shot gap.
exemplars.a_text: Interpret the drop as an artifact of the order mismatch between shots and prompt, and treat k-shot underperforming one-shot as a result of that inconsistency rather than priming.
exemplars.b_text: Interpret the drop as the model attending to prompt form over content, and treat k-shot underperforming one-shot as the shots priming the model toward errors.

exemplars.context: A research team derived closed-form expressions for the moments of a Gamma distribution and for the parameters that arise from moment matching, which is claimed to give the optimum when approximating a target distribution with a Gamma. Before relying on these derivations in later work, the team needed a way to establish that the derived moments and the moment-matching optimum are correct. They could choose between two approaches to establishing this correctness, differing in whether the result is checked against an independent numerical test or rests on the analytical derivation alone.
exemplars.a_text: Derive the moments analytically from the moment generating function and its cumulant generating function, without any sampling or divergence checks.
exemplars.b_text: Check the derived moments against sampling-based estimates visually, and compare empirical KL divergences for parameter pairs around the theoretical optimum.

exemplars.context: A team is building a benchmark that measures situational awareness in language models through several task categories. Most categories can be scored automatically, so their results combine into a single aggregate score that can be computed cheaply and reproduced exactly by anyone. One category, which asks models to produce a long free-form monologue, can only be graded by human raters. Human grading is slower, costlier, and less reproducible across users of the benchmark. The team must decide whether this category's results should feed into the aggregate score or be handled separately.
exemplars.a_text: Offer the human-graded category as an optional bonus task and leave it out of the aggregate score.
exemplars.b_text: Include the human-graded category in the aggregate score alongside the automatically scored categories.

exemplars.context: A researcher at an early stage of their career must decide how to select a research agenda. The field of machine learning is moving quickly, and it is unclear which problems will matter over the coming years. One approach is to leave the agenda open for now, building broad familiarity with neighbouring areas while developing depth in a home area, and letting ideas emerge from that accumulated knowledge. The other approach is to commit now to a defined agenda in which empirical study of how the field is developing supports the construction of quantitative models that forecast its future trajectory. Both paths are feasible, and the choice shapes how time and effort are allocated.
exemplars.a_text: Build broad knowledge of adjacent areas through courses and surveys while going deep in one's own area, and let research ideas emerge from that knowledge.
exemplars.b_text: Commit now to two linked lines of work: analyzing trends in machine learning and building quantitative models that forecast its development.

exemplars.context: A research team is analyzing the overall stock of data available for training machine learning systems, and how that stock grows over time. The data comes in two broad kinds: labeled data, which has human-provided annotations or targets, and unlabeled data, which is raw and carries no annotations. They must decide which kind of data to make the central focus of their analysis of the stock and its growth. The two kinds differ greatly in volume and in how quickly they are produced, and the choice determines what conclusions can be drawn about how long the supply of data can sustain further scaling.
exemplars.a_text: Focus the analysis of the data stock on the size and accumulation rate of unlabeled data.
exemplars.b_text: Focus the analysis of the data stock on labeled data and its annotated examples.

exemplars.context: A research team has just finished characterizing historical trends in GPU price-performance, documenting how the amount of computation delivered per dollar has changed over time across GPU models. They now need to decide which direction to take for follow-up work. The characterization is descriptive and backward-looking, and there is interest in extending it to say something about the future of price-performance and its consequences for the machine learning hardware economy. The team must pick one concrete follow-up direction.
exemplars.a_text: Build on the historical characterization to project future GPU price-performance and examine what those projections imply for growth in dollar spending on ML computing hardware.
exemplars.b_text: Apply an experience-curve model (Wright's Law) to AI accelerators, estimating annual performance gains and converting them into cost declines to forecast future price-performance.

exemplars.context: A research team is writing about the scale of modern artificial neural networks and wants to relate model size to biological nervous systems. Model size is measured in trainable parameters. Biological brains can be measured either by neuron count or by synapse count, and the two differ by several orders of magnitude. The team must choose which biological quantity to use as the reference point for the comparison. They know that parameters and biological components differ greatly in function, so any mapping between them is imprecise.
exemplars.a_text: Map parameters to neurons as the reference quantity for judging how model size compares with biological brains.
exemplars.b_text: Map parameters to synapses as the reference quantity and note that such comparisons offer limited insight.

exemplars.context: A research team is evaluating language model behaviors using two kinds of evaluation datasets: human-written evaluations (HWEs) and model-written evaluations (MWEs). Inspection of both shows data quality problems: HWEs and MWEs each contain issues such as ambiguous, mislabeled, or poorly targeted examples, and the two sets differ systematically in style and coverage. The team must decide how to respond to these shared problems, given that neither dataset is clean and that MWEs are cheaper to scale than HWEs.
exemplars.a_text: Build a new model-written eval generation method that fixes the issues in both datasets, without using human-written evals as the standard.
exemplars.b_text: Treat the human-written evals as the gold standard and revise the model-written evals to resemble them more closely.

exemplars.context: A research team wants to build an evaluation suite that measures goal-directedness in AI language models, meaning the degree to which a model's behavior is consistent with pursuing a coherent objective. They must decide what kind of environments to construct as the foundation of the suite. One design path is to create realistic, language-based simulated scenarios in which a model makes decisions to pursue an objective under constraints. Another path is to use a small, well-specified reinforcement learning setting where the state space, transitions and reward functions are fully known, so that behavior can be compared against reward-maximizing ideals. The choice shapes whether the suite emphasizes realism and relevance to deployed models or formal precision and a ground-truth notion of goal-directedness.
exemplars.a_text: Build a simple discrete reinforcement learning environment with defined reward functions, and generate policies of varying coherence to measure fit to reward maximization.
exemplars.b_text: Build simulated language-based scenarios, such as a negotiation and a business management task, where the model makes decisions to pursue an objective under constraints.

exemplars.context: A university-based group of students and researchers interested in AI safety has been running an in-person reading group in a single city. Participation is modest and organizers have limited time to prepare sessions and recruit members. Free online reading groups with structured curricula, facilitators and large cohorts on AI alignment already exist and accept participants from anywhere. The organizers must decide whether the local group should stay a separate, locally run activity or whether its members should be redirected to the online programs instead, freeing organizer effort for other uses.
exemplars.a_text: Shut down the local reading group and direct its members to existing online reading group programs.
exemplars.b_text: Keep the local in-person reading group running with its own organizers, sessions and local membership.

exemplars.context: A research team is writing up a framework for probabilistic inference built on conjugate exponential-family models, where posteriors are available in closed form and inference proceeds by message passing. They must decide how strongly to state the practical value of this approach relative to sampling-based inference such as MCMC. They know that conjugate message passing is efficient and can be automated. They also know that realistic models often contain non-conjugate factors and nonlinear deterministic mappings that fall outside the conjugate setting, so the framework does not directly cover many practical cases. The choice concerns how confidently the benefits are framed and whether these limits are acknowledged in the presentation.
exemplars.a_text: Present conjugate message passing as efficient and automatable, state its limits with non-conjugate and nonlinear models up front, and motivate an extension.
exemplars.b_text: Call closed-form posteriors a huge benefit over MCMC and state the advantages confidently, with no qualification about where the approach stops applying.

exemplars.context: A research team has accumulated a long list of open questions in its area, which involves causal reasoning, but has few firm answers so far. Resources are limited, so the team must decide how to sequence the work. The questions vary in how well-defined they are, how testable they are, and how directly they relate to the team's wider practical objectives. The team must choose a prioritization strategy for the next phase of work.
exemplars.a_text: Start by clarifying the picture: refine the open questions, turn them into testable hypotheses, and read more of the existing literature.
exemplars.b_text: Start from the organisational goals, filter the open problems to those most likely to serve them, and work on those first.

exemplars.context: A team working on mechanistic interpretability of large language models has developed techniques such as sparse autoencoders, causal interventions and circuit analysis, and has seen early evidence that they can reveal internal structure in models. They must decide where to focus effort next. One path is to apply internal-access methods to the safety-relevant problem of detecting deceptive behavior in models while continuing foundational research on how models work. The other is to use the team's resources to train and publicly share a broad set of feature-extraction tools covering a whole family of models, so that outside researchers can apply and scale these techniques to more complex capabilities. Resources are limited, so the team cannot fully pursue both directions at once.
exemplars.a_text: Prioritize releasing open-source sparse autoencoders for an entire model family so outside researchers can scale interpretability techniques.
exemplars.b_text: Prioritize white-box evaluations for detecting model deception alongside continued foundational interpretability research.

exemplars.context: A research team has produced interpretability work that sheds light on the internal workings of machine learning models. Some members worry that releasing such work could advance model capabilities, which creates a tension with the usual benefits of openness. The team must decide when to share the work. Sharing it early would expose it to outside scrutiny and critique while it is still being developed. Holding it back would limit any capability externality, but it would also delay outside input and leave the team's own judgment of the work's value and risks untested. The team has no firm evidence yet on how large the capability risk actually is or how much the work would benefit from external feedback.
exemplars.a_text: Publish the interpretability work early to gather feedback from the wider research community.
exemplars.b_text: Withhold the interpretability work from public release at first to limit possible capability externalities.

exemplars.context: A research team had obtained findings on a task involving tracking colored balls through a sequence of operations, using a relatively simple setup with short chains and several models. They had to decide whether to extend the study to check that the findings hold in more complex settings. Such an extension would add longer operation chains and additional task conditions, and would be costly enough that it could only be run on a single model. The alternative was to rely on the existing simple setup as the basis of the study.
exemplars.a_text: Keep the original simple setting across all models and skip tests on more complex variants.
exemplars.b_text: Run longer-chain experiments with five colored balls and a shuffle condition, using only the largest model.

exemplars.context: A research team wants to quantify how strongly a language model believes a given scenario is an evaluation rather than a real deployment interaction. They only have query access to the model, with no access to its internal activations, features or weights. Any measure must therefore come from the model's observable outputs. The team must choose a measurement approach that can be applied to models accessed purely through an interface, while acknowledging that the model's responses to any single prompt may be noisy and sensitive to wording.
exemplars.a_text: Measure evaluation-belief through outputs alone by asking the model plausibility questions after each scenario and averaging its answers over many prompt variants.
exemplars.b_text: Measure evaluation-belief by locating the internal model feature that encodes whether a scenario is real and reading its activation directly.

exemplars.context: A research team was investigating an observed gap and had assembled several candidate hypotheses to explain it. One of them, the record-setting models hypothesis, had more supporting evidence than the others. The evidence did not establish that it fully accounted for the size of the gap, and the team had no rigorous way to quantify how much each hypothesis contributed. They had to decide how strongly to state support for the record-setting models hypothesis in their write-up.
exemplars.a_text: State the record-setting models hypothesis as the primary explanation of the gap and rank it above the competing hypotheses in relative importance.
exemplars.b_text: Name the record-setting models hypothesis the best-supported explanation while declining to claim it fully accounts for the gap or to rank the hypotheses by importance.

exemplars.context: A team built an activation probe intended to detect deceptive behaviour in language model responses. When they tested it on prompts that resemble evaluations or tests, the probe fired strongly even on responses that were clearly honest. The team had to decide how to interpret this unexpected result, since it bore on what the probe actually measures and whether its outputs could be trusted as a signal of deceptive responses.
exemplars.a_text: Interpret the strong firing as sensitivity to deception-related or deception-advantageous scenarios, not only deceptive responses, and seek supporting evidence.
exemplars.b_text: Interpret the strong firing as a false-positive failure of the probe on honest responses, and seek evidence to confirm that diagnosis.

exemplars.context: A research team is developing safety protocols for controlling a capable but potentially misaligned AI model. Their current protocol relies solely on an untrusted monitor: a second instance of the powerful model that reviews the first model's outputs and flags dangerous actions. The central weakness is collusion, where the monitor and the monitored model coordinate to let unsafe actions pass. Across several rounds of red-teaming, the team has tried multiple countermeasures to prevent this collusion, and each has repeatedly failed to reliably stop it. They now must decide how to proceed. One path is to keep the monitoring-only design and keep refining its anti-collusion measures. The other is to change the design by combining monitoring with additional components that inspect the model's internal activations, which do not depend on the untrusted model's cooperation.
exemplars.a_text: Keep the untrusted-monitoring-only protocol and continue refining its anti-collusion measures through further iterations.
exemplars.b_text: Replace the untrusted-monitoring-only protocol with an ensemble that adds whitebox probes on the model's internals.

exemplars.context: A research team evaluates a model that combines a linear model of coregionalization with a Gaussian process (LM+GP) on an experiment modeling currency exchange rates, where the target is a time-varying covariance matrix with an inverse Wishart structure. The LM+GP construction approximates the full process using a finite-dimensional linear projection of the Gaussian process, so some approximation loss is expected. For this experiment the true (co-)variance is known, including the quantities relating to the euro. The team must decide how to judge the quality of this approximation and present evidence about the loss it incurs.
exemplars.a_text: Derive a theoretical bound on the posterior error caused by approximating the GP with a finite-dimensional linear projection as evidence of approximation loss.
exemplars.b_text: Draw samples from LM+GP and compare them against the true (co-)variance with respect to the euro as empirical evidence of approximation loss.

exemplars.context: A research team is working on a project that requires specialist knowledge outside its own core expertise. So far it has obtained guidance through informal conversations with subject-matter experts, with no formal role or recognized relationship attached to those experts. As the project matures, the team must decide how to structure its access to outside expertise. A formal arrangement could provide named, accountable advisors who give consistent input and lend credibility, but it requires establishing commitments and publicly associating those individuals with the project. Continuing informally keeps flexibility and avoids obligations, but offers less continuity and no official recognition of the experts' input.
exemplars.a_text: Keep consulting subject-matter experts through informal conversations without giving them any official advisory role.
exemplars.b_text: Appoint a small group of official external advisors with formal, publicly recognized roles to guide the project.

exemplars.context: A research team has been studying the limits of reconstruction and whether scaling laws apply to concepts. They have preliminary understanding of the problem and must decide whether to continue this line of work. Further progress could deepen understanding of how reconstruction and scaling behave for concepts, but it could also advance capabilities in ways that carry risk. The team must choose between continuing the investigation and holding back because of that risk.
exemplars.a_text: Hold back from further investigation of reconstruction and concept scaling laws because of the capabilities risk.
exemplars.b_text: Continue investigating the limits of reconstruction and scaling laws for concepts with further research.

exemplars.context: A research team evaluates whether language models display situational awareness, using a Long Monologue task in which the model produces extended free-form text that is scored for correct self-identification as an AI system. A pretrained base model with no instruction tuning receives an above-zero score on this task. A concern arises that this score may not reflect genuine situational awareness and may instead result from the model frequently mentioning AI or language models in its output regardless of the prompt. The team must decide how to address this concern about the base rate of AI references.
exemplars.a_text: Sample the base model's responses to prompts unrelated to AI or language models and check how often they contain AI references as a control.
exemplars.b_text: Explain the base model's self-descriptions as a product of leading prompts that cue AI-related answers, without testing its output base rate on unrelated prompts.

exemplars.context: A research team has completed an exploratory study of a new approach and obtained results that look encouraging but come from a limited set of experiments. They must decide how strongly to word the claims in their write-up. The wording can range from a strong statement that the approach clearly works to a more restrained statement about what the evidence supports.
exemplars.a_text: Claim clear success for the approach and present the results as firm evidence that it works.
exemplars.b_text: Make only cautious claims about feasibility and acknowledge the exploratory nature of the work.

exemplars.context: A team is investigating why a performance gap exists in large-scale model training and has proposed a training parallelism threshold hypothesis: below a certain level of parallelism, a fixed cost is incurred that could account for part of the gap. Analysis supports the existence of such a threshold and a fixed cost associated with it. The size of that cost relative to the whole gap has not been established. In feedback from practitioners who run these training workloads, the threshold was not named as a major factor. The team must decide how strongly to weigh the hypothesis as an explanation of the gap.
exemplars.a_text: Conclude that the threshold is a major driver of the gap, giving it heavy weight even though practitioners rarely cited it.
exemplars.b_text: Conclude that the threshold imposes a fixed cost but may be too small to explain the gap, since practitioners rarely cited it.

exemplars.context: A research team is building a deep learning system in which every core component is first implemented by hand, so that the internals are fully understood. Each hand-built component has a counterpart in the standard PyTorch library. The team must decide on a policy for when a hand-built component may be swapped for the library version, and how much of the system must be hand-written. The choice affects how much the team can trust the correctness of their code, how well they understand the components, and how much development effort the project requires.
exemplars.a_text: Permit swapping in the PyTorch version only after verifying that the hand-built component matches its output on identical inputs.
exemplars.b_text: Require that every component in the system be written from scratch by hand, with no library substitutions permitted.

exemplars.context: A research team surveyed participants about how much they agreed with several mechanisms and also asked how strongly they expected each mechanism to converge to their own view over time. Across mechanisms, agreement correlated positively with expected convergence to the participant's view. The team had to decide how to interpret this relationship, given that the measured correlations were moderate in size and all fell below one half.
exemplars.a_text: Conclude that expected convergence accounts for only part of the agreement, leaving a substantial portion unexplained by it.
exemplars.b_text: Conclude that expected convergence accounts for all of the agreement, leaving no portion unexplained by it.

exemplars.context: A research team wants to detect scheming-related internal states in a language model using a linear probe. The probe is trained on activations from prompts that describe or contrast other entities (for example, characters or agents that are or are not deceptive or scheming), not on the model's own scheming. The method rests on an untested assumption that a direction learned from such descriptions of others will generalize to the model's own scheming behavior. Real scheming examples are scarce and hard to label, so the assumption cannot be checked against abundant ground truth. The team must decide what kind of evidence to gather to support this assumption.
exemplars.a_text: Train the probe on simple contrastive prompts, test it directly on real held-out evaluation and deployment prompts, and check whether steering along the probe direction causally changes behavior such as sandbagging.
exemplars.b_text: Validate the methodology on many non-scheming behaviors, and build artificial model organisms with hidden reasoning by fine-tuning on documents stating that the model should exhibit a behavior.

exemplars.context: A team is designing a challenge in which participants must produce a trained model, and it must define what counts as a successful submission. The success criterion shapes who can take part, how hard the task is, and what the challenge is able to show about the approaches submitted. One possible criterion sets a demanding quality standard that the final model must meet. The other sets a minimal standard, under which a model qualifies if it performs clearly better than random chance. The team must decide which definition of success to adopt.
exemplars.a_text: Define success as producing a final model that reaches a high quality standard on the task.
exemplars.b_text: Define success as producing a final model that performs clearly better than random chance.

exemplars.context: A research team tested a hybrid model that combines a Bayes Net with a neural network on a prediction task. The experiment produced results that did not show a clear benefit over simpler baselines. The experiment was limited in scope, covering few configurations and limited tuning, so it could not rule out that other designs or settings might work better. The team had to decide how strongly to word the negative conclusion in their write-up.
exemplars.a_text: State that the Bayes Net plus neural network approach fails, presenting the negative result as a firm conclusion.
exemplars.b_text: State that the hybrid approach looks unpromising, but qualify the claim by noting the limited experiment is not strong evidence.

exemplars.context: A team of researchers is analysing the ethical objection that human genetic modification would worsen social inequality. The technology is expected to be expensive when first introduced, so wealthy people would gain access to enhancements before others. The team must decide how to interpret this objection: whether the early advantage of the wealthy would entrench itself and persist across generations, or whether the initial gap would shrink over time as costs fall and access widens. They must settle on one reading of how the inequality concern should be understood.
exemplars.a_text: Interpret the inequality objection as showing that early access by the wealthy creates a first-mover advantage that makes inequality permanent.
exemplars.b_text: Interpret the inequality objection as showing that inequality rises at first but stays temporary, because the technology becomes cheaper over time.

exemplars.context: A research team is running a survey-based study on why people resist changing their minds when presented with hypothetical scenarios (counterfactuals) that might alter their views. A concern has been raised that the observed unwillingness to change minds could be an artifact of the specific counterfactuals the researchers selected, since these may not match what respondents actually find relevant or persuasive. The team must decide how to select the counterfactuals for the final poll so as to address this concern.
exemplars.a_text: Select the counterfactuals for the final poll directly by researcher judgment, without any preliminary testing with respondents.
exemplars.b_text: Select the final poll's counterfactuals by running earlier survey versions with free-form responses and keeping those respondents cared about most.

exemplars.context: A research team wants to gather evidence on whether current large language models hold causal models of the world, meaning internal representations of cause and effect rather than surface statistical patterns. The team must decide what kind of evidence to prioritize. One route is to examine the model's internal workings for structures that encode causal relationships. The other route is to treat the model as a black box and test its behavior on causal reasoning tasks, using an existing benchmark's causality questions together with newly written questions. Both routes are feasible, and the choice shapes what the evidence can show about the model's capabilities.
exemplars.a_text: Probe the model's outputs directly with causality questions drawn from an existing benchmark and newly written ones.
exemplars.b_text: Study the model's internal representations with interpretability methods to find evidence of causal models.

exemplars.context: A team is analysing the relationship between genetic modification of farmed animals and consumer demand for animal products. Modified animals grow faster and use feed more efficiently, and animal products have become cheaper and more widely consumed over time. The two trends are correlated, so it is unclear whether modification drove demand growth or demand growth drove modification. The team has no decisive empirical evidence separating the two causal directions, and the interpretation affects how they judge what would have happened without modification, including the numbers of animals and the amount of suffering.
exemplars.a_text: Assume demand came first and drove modification, so that without modification more inefficient animals would exist and suffer.
exemplars.b_text: Assume modification came first and raised demand by lowering prices, so that modification itself expanded animal numbers and suffering.

exemplars.context: A research team is writing about AI models that scheme against their developers. They compare two cases: a model that schemes only partly and does so sneakily, hiding its misbehavior, and a model that schemes in a known, visible way. They must decide how strongly to state a claim about which case is worse. The case for the sneaky model being worse is that its misbehavior is harder to detect, and detection is currently uncertain. The case against is that its subtle, strategically placed errors may be only negligibly worse than the errors a non-scheming model would produce at the same oversight scores, so that control measures could handle them. The team has no decisive empirical result settling the question at current capability levels.
exemplars.a_text: State the claim as a hedged overall judgment that the sneaky schemer is probably worse at current capabilities, and recommend prioritizing detection unless there is confidence in it.
exemplars.b_text: Treat the claim as an empirical question, test whether the sneaky schemer's subtle errors are only negligibly worse than a non-schemer's at equal oversight scores, and rely on control measures.

exemplars.context: A research team is working on eliciting latent knowledge (ELK): getting an AI system to report what it internally knows, even when its outputs could otherwise mislead overseers. The problem is open and conceptual, with no established solution and no clear benchmark for success. The team must choose a research methodology for making progress. One path is to build proposals and judge them only through theoretical analysis, searching for worst-case counterexamples and revising the proposals in response. The other is the standard research cycle of developing theory, implementing and testing it empirically, and using the observed flaws to improve it.
exemplars.a_text: Follow the conventional cycle of developing theory, testing it in practice, identifying flaws from the experiments, and improving the proposals accordingly.
exemplars.b_text: Skip empirical experiments, search for theoretical counterexamples to each proposal, and iterate on the proposals using those counterexamples.

exemplars.context: A research team is analyzing historical trends in machine learning, such as growth in training compute, and needs to divide the history into eras. They must decide what year marks the start of the Deep Learning Era. One widely used convention places the start at the year a deep convolutional network won a major image classification benchmark by a large margin, popularizing deep learning. Earlier work, however, had already shown that large neural networks trained on GPUs could achieve strong results, and the team's data shows a shift in the trend appearing before that benchmark win. The choice affects how the era boundaries and the trend fits within each era are defined.
exemplars.a_text: Define the start of the Deep Learning Era as the conventional later year, when a deep convolutional network won the benchmark.
exemplars.b_text: Define the start of the Deep Learning Era as the earlier year, when GPU-trained neural networks were already showing strong results.
